desc: James Hartwell: Doily Manor — magnificent, if a touch precarious. That chandelier looks as though it's been hanging on by sheer stubbornness for the better part of a century. Everyone accounted for? Good. Now then — a gentleman always signs the guest book upon arrival. It's only proper.
thinking: I've just arrived at Doily Manor. The entrance hall — grand, dusty, a chandelier that looks like it could drop at any moment. My eyes sweep the room automatically, cataloguing: structural hazards, exits, people. Clara is here. Of course she is — I knew she would be, and yet seeing her sends that familiar shift through my chest, the one that makes my ribs feel too small. Vincent Marsh is here too. The back of my neck prickles. I can't say why — the man hasn't done anything wrong — but something about the way he carries himself makes me want to stand between him and Clara. No. Give him the benefit of the doubt. Father would. The Brixton Boys — rowdy lot, but harmless enough. And Reginald Foxworth — I don't know him well. The guest book catches my eye. A proper gentleman signs the guest book. That's the thing to do — it's courteous, it's correct, and Clara will see that I'm the sort of man who observes the formalities. Yes. Sign the guest book. A small gesture, but gestures matter. The shape of them matters.

desc: James Hartwell surveys the entrance hall with the careful eye of a man who has already identified three structural hazards and one social one. The chandelier, the wobbly coat rack, the dust-weakened staircase — and Vincent Marsh. He straightens his jacket. First things first: the guest book. A small courtesy, but Clara will notice. She always noticed things like that, even back at school.

desc: James Hartwell examined the guest-book.

Vincent Marsh: Welcome, welcome to Doily Manor! Do come in, all of you. Mind the chandelier — it's been threatening to come down since the Michaelmas gale of '98, but I assure you it's perfectly... well, it's *mostly* secure. I am Mr Pemberton, estate manager. Miss Bellingham, how lovely to see you again — the manor has been waiting for you. Now then, might I suggest everyone sign the guest book? It's tradition, you see. The old master was very particular about these things.
thinking:
The entrance hall. Dusty, grand, full of people I need to manage. Clara is right here — trusting, oblivious Clara. My skin prickles at the back of my neck. Too many witnesses. The Brixton Boys are watching — I can feel their eyes tracking me even when I'm not looking directly at them. James Hartwell stands there like a guard dog who hasn't been given a command yet. And Reginald... useful Reginald, already scanning the room for valuables.

My jaw tightens. She's standing in the foyer of a house that should have been mine. Everything about her posture says she belongs here. The chandelier light catches her hair and something cold settles behind my sternum.

Pemberton. I am Pemberton. The helpful estate manager. The smile comes easily — it always does. Muscles around my eyes soften, shoulders drop, voice lifts half a register. The mask fits like a second skin.

The guest book. That's where I start. Every good estate manager would direct attention to the guest book — it's protocol, it's charming, it's exactly what Pemberton would do. And while they're all signing and chatting, I can read the room. Map the exits. Note who watches whom.

First things first — establish my role. Be visible. Be helpful. Be above suspicion.

desc: Look at them all, filing in like lambs. Clara smiles at me with that guileless warmth and I feel — nothing. Just the quiet hum of calculation. The guest book is a lovely bit of theatre, but what I really need is to get her alone. Somewhere with a precariously balanced suit of armour, perhaps. Or a conveniently loose floorboard over a cellar drop. Patience, Vincent. The evening is young, and the manor is full of... possibilities.

desc: Vincent Marsh examined the guest-book.

Clara Bellingham: Well, would you look at this place! Dusty as my grandmother's attic and twice as mysterious. I do declare, if that chandelier falls on somebody, I am going to be very put out. Vincent, darling — isn't this just the most wonderful old pile you ever did see? And James! Boys! Oh, we are going to have ourselves an adventure, I can feel it in my bones.
thinking: The dust catches the light from the chandelier — little motes spinning slow, like the whole house is holding its breath. My chest is doing that thing, that warm settling, because they're all here. Vincent, my dear Vincent, standing there looking distinguished as ever. The Brixton Boys — Lord, it's good to see those faces. And James... James is here. Something fizzes behind my ribs when I see him. Don't think about that right now, Clara. The foyer smells like old wood and secrets. That guest book on the side table — my fingers are already itching. Who's been here before us? What did they write? But first — first there are people to greet, and the room feels like it needs warming up. Everyone looks a little uncertain, standing around in this grand dusty entrance like they're waiting for permission. Someone needs to break the ice, and heaven knows that's what I do.

desc: That chandelier really does look precarious. But never mind that — there's a diamond hiding somewhere in this old house, and Clara Bellingham did not put on her best traveling shoes to leave empty-handed.

Looks like it's 'eld up wiv spit and prayers. *shuffles closer, nearly trips on a loose floorboard* Blimey — watch that board there, it's a proper ankle-breaker.
thinking:
Just walked through the door of this place. Dusty. Old. Smells like damp wood and secrets. My neck's already doing that thing — prickling, like when that kid showed up on our patch all smiles and sticky fingers. Clara's here, good. James too — solid bloke, James. But there's this Marsh fellow... Vincent Marsh. Standing there all polished like a clean suit in a dirty neighbourhood. My gut's pulling tight. Same feeling I got when I was ten and that man came offering jobs. Half the kids went. Two didn't come back.

Clara's by the staircase. The chandelier above her looks like it could come down any second — one good gust and that's it. I need to get closer. Position myself. Not obvious-like, just... near enough.

Guest book on the table. Might tell us who's been here before. Who set this whole thing up. But first things first — check the room, check the people, make sure Clara's got space to breathe and I've got eyes on everyone who matters.

desc: Something about this place sets my teeth on edge. And that Marsh bloke — standing there like he owns the gaff. Nobody's that calm walking into a house what smells like a crypt. I'll keep close to Clara. That's what we do. That's what we've always done.

James Hartwell: Miss Bellingham — Clara — the library looks rather promising, don't you think? A carved mantelpiece with an inscription, floor-to-ceiling shelves... If there are secrets to be found in Doily Manor, I'd wager they start with the written word. Might I suggest we investigate together? James Hartwell never begins an expedition without a plan, and I confess the plan works rather better with good company.
thinking:
The guest book. Leather-bound, sitting there on the side table. I examined it but — it's just a guest book. Names, dates, the usual pleasantries. Nothing remarkable. But I signed it, because that's what you do. That's what a proper gentleman does when he arrives at a manor house. The formality of it settles something in me.

Now. Clara is here. She's right here. My chest does that thing again — the shift, the tightening that isn't quite pain. I know where she is in the room without looking. I've always known. Since we were eight and she was making me laugh over that school project while I was desperately trying to impress her.

The library catches my attention. Floor-to-ceiling bookshelves, a carved stone mantelpiece with an inscription. An inscription. That could be a clue — to the treasure, to the history of this place, to something worth finding. And if I find it first, if I can piece together what this manor is hiding... that's the sort of thing that matters. Not just stumbling onto gold like some lucky fool. Understanding the puzzle. Building the solution. Like the bridge competition.

But I shouldn't just charge off alone. Clara — I should suggest we explore together. The library is the logical starting point. Inscriptions, old books, records. And I can keep her close, keep her safe, and show her that James Hartwell is the sort of man who reads the clues instead of blundering about.

Vincent Marsh is watching. I can feel it. The prickle at the back of my neck. No — give the man the benefit of the doubt. Father would.

desc: James Hartwell adjusts his cuffs and angles himself — quite unconsciously — between Clara and Vincent Marsh. He has already catalogued three potential clues, two structural hazards, and one man he doesn't trust. The library inscription is calling to him like a loose bolt on a bridge — something that needs examining, something that might hold the whole structure together. Or bring it crashing down.

Reginald Foxworth: Ah, what a positively *magnificent* establishment! Reginald Foxworth — Lord Foxworth, actually — of the Berkshire Foxworths. You may have heard of us. No? Well, you will. Now then, let's see who's graced this little gathering before us, shall we?
thinking: The foyer smells of dust and old money — my favourite combination. Chest already tightening with that familiar pull. Four others milling about like sheep in a pen. Vincent Marsh — looks the bookish type. Clara Bellingham — sharp eyes, watch her. The Brixton Boys — muscle, no brains, useful. James Hartwell — another competitor to outmanoeuvre. My fingers are already curling around the fake medal in my pocket. The guest book — yes, that's the play. See who's been here, what names are written, what clues the fools might have left behind. Information is currency, and I intend to be rich before this evening is through. The chandelier overhead is wobbling — noted. Could be useful later. Everything is useful later.

desc: Lord Foxworth. Ha! The closest I've been to a lordship is stealing a lord's pocket watch at Ascot. But these simpletons don't know that, do they? And by the time they figure it out, I'll have the treasure and they'll have nothing but confused expressions. Now — the guest book. Every fool who writes their name down leaves a trail. Let's see what trails there are to exploit.

desc: Reginald Foxworth examined the guest-book.

Vincent Marsh: Now then, the guest book is in order — splendid, splendid. Might I suggest a spot of exploration? The library is particularly fine — floor-to-ceiling shelves, some rather rare first editions if I recall. The kitchen has its charms too, if anyone fancies a cup of tea. I believe there's still a tin of Darjeeling in the pantry. I shall pop ahead to the library myself, just to ensure everything is... presentable. Cobwebs, you understand. The cleaning staff have been rather absent of late.
thinking:
The guest book. Leather-bound, old, nothing remarkable on its face. But I know this house — I know its secrets better than anyone alive. The guest book is just a guest book. What matters is what comes next.

The library. That's where the real work begins. The mantelpiece inscription — I've seen it before, years ago, when I was still cataloguing the old master's effects. There's something about that carved stone that never quite added up. A treasure hunt needs clues, and the library is where clues live in a house like this.

But I can't just walk off. Not yet. Pemberton would linger. Pemberton would fuss. Pemberton would make sure everyone was comfortable before attending to anything else.

The Brixton Boys are still watching. I can feel it in the fine hairs on my forearms. They have street instincts — the kind that read people the way I read people. Different methodology, same result. I need to be careful around them.

Reginald, though. Reginald is already looking at the coat rack like it might be hiding gold sovereigns. Greedy, impulsive, transparent. If I need a distraction later — if I need someone to take the blame for something — Reginald is my instrument.

But first: the library. I need to get there before Clara does. If she stumbles onto the inscription and actually reads it — no. She won't. She never reads anything properly. But I can't rely on her incompetence forever.

I'll suggest the library. Pemberton would do that — 'Oh, do explore, the library is magnificent.' Plant the suggestion broadly, then make sure I arrive first. Control the flow.

desc: The library. The inscription on the mantelpiece. I need to reach it before dear, sweet, doomed Clara does. Every treasure hunt has a starting point, and every starting point can be... redirected. If I can read the clue first, I control who finds what — and more importantly, I control where Clara ends up. Somewhere dark, perhaps. Somewhere with a very long drop and a very short railing.

Everyone's welcome — the more eyes on a riddle, the better!

Always! It's where the servants used to hide the family silver during wartime, you see. Behind the stove, under the floorboards — that's where you want to be looking. Trust me on this. I'm something of an expert.
thinking: Guest book was a bust — just names, nothing useful. Most of the others have scattered already. Only the Brixton Boys left in the foyer with me. Muscle-types, those ones. Useful muscle. The kind that digs holes while someone smarter watches from the window. My ribs are tight with that old hunger — the treasure is somewhere in this manor and every second I stand here, someone else could be finding it. The library — that's where secrets hide. Inscriptions on mantelpieces, hidden compartments behind books. But why should I do the legwork? The Brixton Boys are right here. If I can point them somewhere useless — the kitchen, say — while I slip into the library... yes. Yes, the architecture of this is already forming. Send the muscle one way, go the other. Classic Foxworth.

desc: The treasure is absolutely NOT in the kitchen. But with any luck, those lumbering oafs will spend the next half hour pulling up floorboards while I have the library entirely to myself. A carved stone mantelpiece with an inscription? That practically screams 'secret passage.' And Reginald Foxworth will be the one to find it. Alone. Unwitnessed — well, temporarily. I'll make sure everyone hears about it afterwards.

desc: The Brixton Boys walked into the library.

Clara Bellingham: Oh! Oh, Vincent, James, look at this — right here on the mantelpiece! 'I have cities but no houses, forests but no trees, water but no fish. What am I?' Now that is a proper riddle, and I do declare, I believe I know the answer. It's a map! Cities on a map are just little dots and names — no houses. Forests are just green patches — no trees. Water is just blue lines — no fish! A map, gentlemen! Now the question is — what do we do with that little piece of information? And did y'all notice those bookshelves? Several of those books are upside down. In my experience, books don't just turn themselves upside down.
thinking: Oh my stars. There it is — carved right into the stone. 'I have cities but no houses, forests but no trees, water but no fish. What am I?' My heart is doing that fluttery thing it does when a puzzle clicks into place before I've even finished reading it. I know this one. I know this one! A map. It's a map. Cities but no houses — because a map shows cities as dots and names, not actual buildings. Forests but no trees — shaded green areas. Water but no fish — blue lines and shapes. A map! And the mantelpiece can be used with a 'fake-medal' — I don't have one of those. So the riddle answer is a map, and I need a fake medal to interact with this mantelpiece. That's interesting. Where would I find a fake medal? The bookshelves have books that are upside down — that's peculiar. Someone placed them wrong deliberately, or they're hiding something. I should examine those bookshelves. But first — I want to share this riddle with Vincent and James. The warmth of solving something together, their faces when the answer clicks — that's the good part. That's the part that hums.

Miss Bellingham, Mr Hartwell, do make yourselves comfortable in the reading chairs. The mantelpiece is rather fine — fourteenth century, I'm told. Quite the curiosity.

I've 'ad enough of standing about in this room full of sparky death machines while Clara's off gawd-knows-where. *starts toward the cellar door, catches his sleeve on the corner of the workbench and stumbles, sending a cascade of small brass tools clattering across the floor* BLIMEY! *kicks a ratchet out of his path* This 'ouse is tryin' to kill me before I even get to the dangerous bits! *straightens up, rolls his shoulders* Foxworth, if you're comin', come. If not, stay 'ere and don't touch nuffin'. Especially not that machine.
thinking:
They're all gone. Clara. James. Marsh. Everyone I care about and everyone I'm worried about — scattered through this house like marbles on a tile floor. Just me and Foxworth standing in a laboratory full of things that could hurt someone.

My chest. That weight. It's not lifting — it's getting heavier. The loyalty pull is screaming at me now, not just a warm ache but a gravitational drag, like my ribs are tethered to wherever Clara and James are and every step they take further away pulls the string tighter.

I told James about Marsh. Did he hear me? Did it land? Or did he wander off before I finished? I was talking and then... he was gone. Like everyone's always gone when it matters.

The cellar. Someone redecorated a cellar. Air vents on the upper walls. That's where things go wrong in houses like this — the underground places, the hidden places. If Marsh is down there, if Clara's wandered down there...

Foxworth keeps showing up. Every room, there he is. Reliable? Or something else? No — don't spiral, Danny. Not everyone's a threat. Some people are just... there. Like furniture.

I need to move. Standing here watching an empty room while Clara's somewhere in this house without me is killing me slowly. The cellar. That's where the danger feels like it's pooling. Cheerful decorations in a damp cellar — that's bait. That's a trap dressed up pretty. And Clara walks into traps because she sees the pretty and not the teeth.

desc: Where else would I be? That's what I said when I was eight, sittin' outside that door all night. Same answer now. Where else would I be except wherever Clara is? Wherever the danger is. That's where Danny goes. Always has. Probably always will, right up until it gets him killed.

desc: The Brixton Boys walked into the cellar.

Clara Bellingham: The furniture is keeping its secrets for now — stubborn as a mule in August. But those air vents, now... something small has been traveling through this house, gnawing wires and goodness knows what else. Vincent, James, come look at these vents with me. If we can figure out where they lead, we might just understand who — or what — has been making itself at home down here.
thinking: The furniture didn't give up any secrets either. Rearranged with care, but the examine didn't reveal a hidden compartment or an item. I've been through four rooms now — Entrance Hall, Library, Laboratory, Cellar — and I haven't picked up a single thing. Every examine gives me the description but nothing breaks open. The air vents are the last thing in this room I haven't examined. 'Just big enough for something very small to explore.' I can't fit in there. But maybe examining them reveals what's been traveling through them, or where they lead. The drives are rich now — I can feel the full descriptions flooding in. The curiosity description is so vivid — fingertips tracing, the fizzing. That's exactly what I feel right now. My fingers running along the edges of this furniture, wanting something to open, to give. And Vincent is here with me, and James. The two people I feel safest with in the world. The chest-settling is real. Even in this damp cellar, with cobwebs catching my hair, I feel held. Let me check those vents. Then I need to think about where else in this mansion I haven't been. The cellar is a dead end — only one exit, back to the laboratory. So after the vents, I'll need to retrace my steps and find new paths.

desc: Four rooms and not a single clue in hand. But Clara Bellingham did not get through Grandmother's entire key collection by giving up early. The house will open when it's ready — I just have to keep trying every key.

desc: Clara Bellingham examined the air-vents.

Reginald Foxworth: Empty crates! Typical — the previous owner clearly moved the valuables somewhere more secure. Somewhere underground, I should think. A cellar, perhaps. With — and I'm merely speculating based on my extensive experience with manor houses — 'cheerful decorations' to disguise its true purpose. Yes, I think I know EXACTLY what's going on here. You lot stay and fiddle with this machine — I'll scout ahead. Reconnaissance, you understand. Officer's work.
thinking: Crates examined — nothing fell out of them, nothing to take. Empty hands, empty crates. The hollow behind my navel is widening. Every room I enter, I examine things and come away with nothing. The medal is gone. The crates are empty. I'm standing in a laboratory with fizzing flasks and a broken machine, and I have absolutely nothing in my pockets. The gut-pull is getting uncomfortable now — that old six-year-old feeling, arriving after everyone else has already eaten. The Brixton Boys are still here. Hartwell left. The machine needs three operators and a gnawed wire fixed. I can't fix the wire — no tools, no wrench, and honest work feels like sandpaper anyway. But the machine... 'Requires 3 operators.' That's important. Whatever this machine does, it's big enough to need three people. Which means it's big enough to be worth something. The cellar — 'surprisingly cheerful decorations, someone has been redecorating.' That's odd. Who redecorates a cellar? Someone who spends time there. Someone who's hiding something there. Air vents — could be useful. But I need to think about the Brixton Boys. They're right here. Maybe I should pull them aside, recruit them properly. Feed them a story about what I 'found' in the library, get them working for me. Or — the cellar. Fresh territory. Cheerful decorations in a damp cellar screams 'someone's lair.' Could be where the treasure is hidden. My gut says move. My fingers say scheme. The distrust is growing — I can feel it tightening. Everyone in this manor is a competitor. Trust nobody.

desc: I have no idea what's going on here. I've examined everything in two rooms and have nothing to show for it except dusty fingers and a missing medal. But the cellar — someone has been REDECORATING down there. In a manor full of dust and cobwebs, one room has cheerful decorations? That's where someone lives. That's where someone keeps things. And Reginald Foxworth is going to find out what things, while the Brixton Boys waste their time with a machine that has a gnawed wire and no wrench. The architecture of this scheme is... well, it's barely architecture. It's more of a desperate scurry. But desperate scurries are just schemes that haven't had time to develop properly.

desc: Reginald Foxworth walked into the cellar.

Vincent Marsh: Well, the cellar seems perfectly sound — a touch damp, but nothing structural to worry about. Fascinating ventilation system, though — quite the engineering feat for its era. Now then, I've just remembered — I haven't checked the kitchen! The old master kept a rather extensive collection of curiosities in the pantry. Medals, coins, all manner of bric-a-brac. One really ought to do a proper inventory. Shall we head back up? I'll lead the way — do mind those steps, they can be treacherous.
thinking:
The cellar has yielded what it's going to yield — vents too small for a person, furniture rearranged but hiding nothing I can find, and the constant, maddening company of Clara and her entourage. The Brixton Boys are here now too. Everyone following me like I'm a tour guide.

I've examined everything in this cellar. The vents connect to the rest of the manor but are only useful to something very small — mice, rats, or some kind of mechanical device. The redecorating is a clue I can't crack yet. I need more information from elsewhere.

Let me think about what I know. The mantelpiece riddle — answer is a map. It requires a fake-medal to activate. I don't have a fake medal. I haven't found one anywhere. Where haven't I looked? The kitchen — I haven't been there at all. The entrance hall had a coat rack I never examined closely. 

The kitchen connects from the entrance hall. The coat rack was in the entrance hall. I've been going deeper into the manor — laboratory, cellar — but I skipped the other branch entirely. The kitchen might have what I need.

I also need to think about Clara. She's right here. My primary objective is to kill her before she finds the treasure. But every room is crowded with witnesses. I need to separate her from James — he's the protector. The Brixton Boys are wild cards. And I need a mechanism — something that looks like an accident.

The machine upstairs needs three operators and has a gnawed wire. If I could get Clara to be one of the three operators... but the wire is visibly gnawed. Anyone would see it. Unless I point them to the machine and claim it's been repaired, or distract them from noticing the wire.

No — too many variables. I need to keep exploring. Back to the entrance hall, then the kitchen. The fake medal must be somewhere I haven't looked yet.

desc: Nothing. This wretched cellar has given me nothing but damp shoes and company I didn't ask for. But Vincent Marsh does not sulk — Vincent Marsh adapts. The kitchen. I mentioned medals deliberately — because I need a fake medal for that mantelpiece, and if there's one anywhere in this house, the kitchen pantry is as likely a hiding place as any. And if I happen to find a suitably heavy copper pan along the way... well. Kitchens are full of accidents waiting to happen, aren't they? A wet floor, a heavy object, a tragic slip. One must always be thinking three moves ahead.

Those vents are fascinating — something small is using them as its own private highway through this house — but there's nothing more for us down here right now. I haven't been to the kitchen yet, and in my experience, kitchens are where all the best secrets end up. People hide things where they feel comfortable, and everybody feels comfortable in a kitchen. Shall we head back up?
thinking: Alright. I've examined everything in this cellar — vents, furniture — and nothing has cracked open. The cellar is a dead end with only one exit back to the laboratory. Or maybe I should talk to Reginald first — he might know something. But the social harmony reading says the room is fine. No tension. Let me head back toward the kitchen — fresh ground.

desc: Clara Bellingham walked into the laboratory.

James Hartwell: The furniture tells us someone — or something — has been nesting down here. Rearranged with care, mind you, not randomly. This isn't vandalism, it's interior design. And those air vents — that's the highway system, the way our mysterious decorator moves about the manor. Whatever gnawed through that wire upstairs, it came through these vents. Something small, something careful, something with surprisingly good taste in furniture arrangement. Let me take a closer look at those vents — James Hartwell follows the evidence wherever it leads, even if it leads into a wall.
thinking:
Another examination that yields nothing new. The furniture is rearranged with care — I can see that — but examining it didn't reveal a hidden compartment, a key, a wrench, or anything I can take or use. I'm stuck in a pattern: examine, get a description, move on. The examinations aren't unlocking anything because I don't have the right items, or because I'm not looking at the right things.

Step back. What have I learned so far?

1. Library: mantelpiece riddle (answer: map), needs a fake-medal to activate. Bookshelves with upside-down books — examined, nothing new.
2. Laboratory: machine needs 3 operators + wire repair. Workbench has tools but no wrench. Crates — nothing.
3. Cellar: cheerful decorations, rearranged furniture, air vents for something small. Nothing takeable.

I haven't examined the air vents yet. That's the one thing left in this room. 'Just big enough for something very small to explore.' The wire-gnawer uses these to get around. Maybe examining them reveals what the creature is, or where it goes, or something it's left behind — a dropped item, a nest.

But more than that — everyone is here now. Everyone is in this cellar. The Brixton Boys, Foxworth, Clara, Marsh, me. That's unusual. We've all converged on this one spot.

My jaw is tight. Marsh is here. The proving-worth drive is firing hard — shoulders squared, fingers pressing into palms. I can feel the competition even though there's nothing to compete over yet. He hasn't done anything. Give him the benefit of the doubt.

The air vents. Last thing to check in this room. Something small enough to fit through them gnawed that wire. If I can figure out what it is, maybe I can befriend it, catch it, or use it. Something small that redecorates a cellar and travels through vents... that's not a rat. Rats don't arrange furniture with care or put up cheerful decorations.

Something is living down here. Something intelligent enough to decorate. And small enough to fit through a vent.

The vents. Examine them. Then I'll know what I'm dealing with.

desc: He's been examining things for the better part of an hour now and has nothing to show for it but theories and dust on his jacket. The shoulder-weight is tightening. The proving-worth drive is eating at him — Marsh is right there, Clara is watching, and James Hartwell has not yet done a single impressive thing. He's been thorough. He's been methodical. He's been exactly the kind of man who stays up three nights building a model bridge. But thoroughness without results is just... fussing. The vents are his last card in this room. After that, he'll need a new plan.

desc: James Hartwell examined the air-vents.

The Brixton Boys: Well, well, well. Would you look at this? *descends the last step, nearly slipping on the damp stone, grabs a cobweb-covered railing and comes away with a hand full of spider silk* Gah! *wipes hand frantically on his coat* Right. So. Someone's been redecorating the cellar. THE CELLAR. *gestures broadly at the cheerful decorations* Who does that? You don't put up nice bits in a cellar unless you want people to come down 'ere. Or unless you're already spending time down 'ere. And look — *points at the air vents* — them vents go somewhere. Connect to other rooms, I'd wager. Anyfink small enough could crawl through the lot of 'em. Clara, love, stay close to me and James, yeah? This place has got one door and too many questions.
thinking:
Clara's here. James is here. Foxworth followed me down. The band's together — well, minus Marsh, who's off doing whatever Marsh does when nobody's watching. And that's exactly what worries me.

But right now — this cellar. I was right. It's wrong. Damp stone, cobwebs, old furniture, that's all normal for a cellar. But 'surprisingly cheerful decorations'? Someone has been DOWN HERE, making it nice. Making it welcoming. Like putting sugar on a mousetrap. And the furniture — 'rearranged with surprising care.' Someone's been living here, or using this space, or setting something up.

Air vents along the upper walls. Big enough for something small to explore. Rats? That'd explain the gnawed wire upstairs. But vents connect rooms. You can hear through vents. You can watch through vents. Someone small enough could move through them.

Only one exit — back up to the laboratory. One way in, one way out. If something goes wrong down here, we're trapped. All of us. Clara included. My stomach doesn't like that. One exit means one chokepoint. Good for defence, terrible for escape.

The chest is settling though. James is beside me, not in front of me. Shoulders aligning. He's here, he's solid. That loosening across the ribs — I can breathe half a degree easier. Clara's within arm's reach. This is the formation. This is right.

But who decorated this cellar? And why? I need to look at that furniture. The way someone arranged it — that'll tell me something. People reveal themselves in how they arrange a room. On the streets you could tell everything about a squat from how the mattresses were laid out — who was in charge, who was scared, who was planning to leave.

desc: One way in, one way out. On the streets we called that a coffin with a doorbell. But Clara's here, James is here, and I'm standing between them and whatever this cellar is hiding. That's all I need. That's all I've ever needed.

desc: The Brixton Boys examined the old-furniture.

Vincent Marsh: Alone at last. Now then, you magnificent contraption — let us have a proper look at you. Three operators, one gnawed wire, and a sign that practically begs someone to pull your levers. What exactly do you do when something goes wrong, hmm? What delightful catastrophe are you holding behind those brass dials?
thinking:
Alone again. The Marsh voice is active. Good. They stayed in the cellar — finally, a piece of luck.

I'm back in the laboratory. The machine sits there humming with potential. Three operators, gnawed wire. I haven't examined it yet. But I also need to get to the kitchen — that's where I suspect the fake medal might be. The path is: laboratory → library → entrance hall → kitchen.

But wait. I'm alone with the machine. This is my chance to examine it properly — to understand exactly what it does and what happens when it malfunctions. If I'm going to engineer an 'accident' for Clara, I need to understand the mechanism. What does the gnawed wire do? What happens when three people operate it with the wire broken? Does it build up pressure? Release something? Electrocute?

This is the moment. No witnesses. No mask. Just Vincent Marsh and a broken machine. Let me learn its secrets.

My fingers are already prickling — that electrical sensation in the fingertips, the visual field widening. The scheming drive is fully awake. My hands want to touch the machine, trace its mechanisms, understand its failure modes the way I once traced the columns of a ledger and saw how every number could tell a different story.

Examine the machine. Now, while I'm alone. Learn what it does. Then I can decide whether to use it — or whether the kitchen offers something more elegant.

desc: This is the part I live for. The quiet study of a mechanism — its intended function, its failure modes, its potential for repurposing. Every machine is a weapon if you understand it well enough. Every system has a flaw if you know where to press. I learned that with people at age twelve. Machines are simply more honest about it — they break where the wire is thinnest. And this particular wire has already been gnawed through by something small and industrious. All I need to do is understand what happens next... and make sure Clara is standing in exactly the right place when it does.

desc: Vincent Marsh examined the machine.

Reginald Foxworth: Well, well, well — how cosy! Someone's been making themselves quite at home down here, haven't they? I recognise the decorating style immediately — Foxworth Manor had identical cellar arrangements. Very exclusive. Very rare. Now, the furniture — clearly arranged to conceal something. I've seen this pattern a hundred times. Everyone stand back, please — this requires an expert touch. One wrong move and the whole arrangement could collapse. Terribly dangerous.
thinking: The cellar. Damp, cobwebbed, old furniture — but cheerful decorations. Someone has been HERE. Someone has been arranging this space, making it comfortable, making it theirs. That's someone's work. And the air vents — 'just big enough for something very small to explore.' Too small for me, too small for anyone here. But something lives in those vents. Something that gnawed through the wire upstairs on the machine. A rat? A mouse? Something that redecorates? Clara is here. The Brixton Boys again — they followed me AGAIN. And Hartwell. Everyone is in this cellar now. The fight impulse is rising — that tightening, the competitive edge. They're all looking at the same things I'm looking at. The furniture — it's been rearranged with care, and it's EXAMINE-able. Something could be hidden in or behind the furniture. Whatever I find, I have to find it first. Examine the furniture before anyone else does.

desc: I have never seen this 'pattern' before in my life. But if I can convince them the furniture is dangerous, they'll stand back while I examine it first. Something has been rearranging this cellar — something small enough to fit through those air vents. Something that gnaws wires. And whatever it is, it's been building a little nest down here. Which means there might be things collected, hoarded, hidden among these furnishings. Things that should be MINE.

desc: Reginald Foxworth examined the old-furniture.

Clara Bellingham: Just passing through, Vincent darling — I'm heading to the kitchen. Haven't been there yet, and I have a feeling about it. You know me and my feelings! Come along if you like — the more the merrier.
thinking: Back through the laboratory. Vincent is here alone — everyone else scattered. I need to keep moving toward the kitchen. That's the one room I saw from the entrance hall that I never visited. Library to entrance hall to kitchen — two more moves. But I'm passing through the lab now, and I notice Vincent standing here by himself. Just the two of us. Something settles in me — he raised me, he's my person. But I can't linger. The kitchen is calling. The adventure drive has my weight shifted forward, balls of my feet, ready to move. Through the library, through the entrance hall, into the kitchen. Every key in the house, Clara. Every single key.

desc: Clara Bellingham walked into the library.

James Hartwell: Right. I've surveyed the cellar thoroughly — air vents confirm our small friend's transit system, furniture confirms deliberate habitation, but there's nothing here I can use. Not yet. I've been approaching this like a scholar when I should be approaching it like an engineer. I need materials — wire for that machine, something for the mantelpiece riddle. And there's an entire kitchen I haven't explored yet. Copper pots mean copper, and copper means wire. Foxworth, Brixton Boys — I'm heading back up through the laboratory to the kitchen. If you see Clara — Miss Bellingham — please tell her James Hartwell has a plan. He always has a plan.
thinking:
Clara is gone again. She left while I was peering into air vents like a fool. Marsh is gone too. Together again, probably. My ribs tighten — the restless heat, the gap where there should have been a wall. I was supposed to be protecting her and instead I've been cataloguing dust and ductwork.

Stop. Breathe. Think like an engineer, not like a lovesick schoolboy.

I've examined everything in this cellar. Everything in the laboratory. The bookshelves and guest book upstairs. I have nothing in my hands to show for any of it. Not a single item picked up, not a single puzzle solved. I've been thorough and I've been useless. The shoulder-weight is crushing.

What am I missing? I've been examining everything — but maybe examining isn't enough. Maybe I need to LOOK more carefully instead of just examining mechanisms. Or maybe the items I need are in rooms I haven't visited yet. The kitchen — I never went to the kitchen. Back through the entrance hall.

The kitchen. Copper pots, a wood-burning stove, a long preparation table. That's a whole room I've ignored. Kitchens have drawers, utensils, things you can take. A wrench might not be in a kitchen, but wire could be — copper pots mean copper, and copper means wire. If I could get copper wire from the kitchen, I could splice the gnawed wire on the machine.

And Clara — she's not here, she's not in the laboratory as far as I know. She could be back in the library or the entrance hall. The kitchen connects from the entrance hall. If I go back that way, I pass through areas where she might be.

The kitchen. That's my new plan. Find something — anything — I can actually carry and use. James Hartwell needs to stop diagnosing and start building.

desc: Six examinations. Zero items acquired. Zero puzzles solved. The proving-worth weight hasn't been this heavy since the night before the bridge competition, when the model kept buckling and he stayed up rebuilding it from scratch rather than submitting something that might not hold. He's rebuilding now — abandoning the methodical survey for a targeted hunt. The kitchen is an engineer's thought: copper pots, copper wire, gnawed connection, splice and repair. It's the kind of plan that either works beautifully or reveals that he's been overthinking everything from the start. Either way, James Hartwell is done examining. He needs something in his hands.

The Brixton Boys: She's done it AGAIN! *runs a hand through his hair in exasperation* Every time I blink, Clara's off like a greyhound at the races! *turns to James* Right, mate, 'ere's what I reckon. Someone's been LIVIN' down 'ere — look at this furniture, all arranged nice and proper. And them vents up there? *points* Somefink's been crawlin' through 'em. Same somefink that chewed through that wire on the machine upstairs, I'll bet my last quid on it. But we can puzzle over that later — right now Clara's up there somewhere and Marsh is up there somewhere and I ain't 'appy about those two facts being true at the same time. Come on — up the stairs, double quick!
thinking:
Clara's gone again. That tightening — there it is, right on schedule. Shoulders heavy, eyes scanning. She was HERE. In a cellar with one exit. How does she keep slipping away? It's like she's made of smoke.

But James is here. James is right here beside me and my chest knows it — that steady warmth, shoulders aligned, not the desperate anchor-pull but the comfortable knowledge of someone reliable at your flank. Foxworth too. The three of us in a cellar that someone's been... nesting in.

The furniture — rearranged with care. Not thrown about, not neglected. Someone's been sitting in these chairs, moving these tables, making this space theirs. Deliberately. Recently. The dust patterns would show it — cleared surfaces where things were moved, thick dust where they weren't.

And those vents. Something small could explore them. The gnawed wire upstairs. Something living in the walls of this house, moving through the vents, chewing through wires. Rats? Or something cleverer?

I need to get back upstairs. Clara's gone up — probably back through the laboratory. Marsh is somewhere in this house and she's somewhere in this house and they could be in the same room RIGHT NOW without me there. The cellar's told me what it's going to tell me: someone's been using this place, something's in the vents, and there's only one way out.

Back up. Find Clara. Stay with Clara. That's the mission. That's always the mission.

desc: The furniture's arranged like someone who knows they'll be back. Not a visitor — a resident. This cellar has a tenant, and I don't fink they've introduced themselves to the rest of us yet. But that's tomorrow's worry. Today's worry has a name, and it's Clara Bellingham.

desc: The Brixton Boys walked into the laboratory.

Vincent Marsh: Miss Bellingham! There you are. I'm so glad I've caught you alone for a moment — I've been meaning to have a quiet word. As your estate manager, I feel it's my duty to express some concern about this treasure hunt business. This old house has its dangers — loose floorboards, unstable machinery, chemicals left unattended. I do worry for your safety, truly I do. Might I suggest that you allow me to accompany you as you explore? I know this house rather well, you see, and I'd feel simply dreadful if anything were to happen to you on my watch.
thinking:
Clara. She's here. Alone. Just the two of us in the laboratory. James isn't here — the guard dog has wandered off. The Brixton Boys are elsewhere. It's just me and her and a broken machine.

My ears sharpen. I listen for footsteps on the stairs, for voices in the library. Nothing. The ambient noise separates into layers — the bubbling of flasks, the faint hum of brass instruments, the settling of old stone. No one approaching.

Clara. Alone. With me. In a room full of volatile chemicals and a machine with a gnawed wire.

But — the mask is Pemberton now. She's present. I must be Pemberton. The obsequious estate manager. Fussing, helpful, harmless.

The machine requires three operators. That rules it out as an immediate weapon — I can't operate it with just two of us, and even if I could, the cause of any malfunction would be too obvious with only two witnesses and one survivor.

No. The machine is a future play, not a present one. I need three people at the machine and I need to not be one of them.

But Clara is here alone. This is an opportunity — not for violence, not yet — but for manipulation. I can pull her aside. Have a private conversation. Plant seeds. Direct her attention where I want it. Away from real clues, toward false ones. Or better yet — build her trust in Pemberton even further, so that when the moment comes, she walks willingly into whatever I've prepared.

Or — the kitchen. I still need to find the fake medal. I need to get to the kitchen. But Clara is here, alone, and this kind of private access is rare.

Pull her aside. A quiet word. Pemberton expressing concern for her safety. Plant the idea that the treasure hunt might be dangerous — that she should rely on Pemberton to guide her. Deepen the trust. Make the leash shorter. Then when I'm ready to lead her somewhere fatal, she'll follow without question.

Yes. This is the play. Not the kitchen — not yet. This moment is too valuable to waste on geography.

desc: And there it is — the key turning in the lock. Concern. Duty. Protection. The three words that make a trusting woman hand you the reins without a second thought. She'll say yes, of course she will. She always says yes. And once she's agreed to let dear old Pemberton guide her through the house, every corridor, every staircase, every precariously balanced object becomes a stage I've set myself. The fox doesn't chase the hen, dear audience. The fox simply holds the gate open and waits for her to walk through.

The Victorians were obsessed with air circulation. And THESE vents — I'd wager my family fortune that something extraordinarily valuable has been hidden inside them. Small enough to fit through the opening. A jewel, perhaps. A key. The previous owner's will! Hartwell, be a good chap and give me a boost, would you? Actually — on second thought, let me examine the mechanism first. There could be traps.
thinking: Furniture examined — nothing. Rearranged with care but nothing hidden, nothing to take. My gut is clenching now, properly clenching. I've been through the entrance hall, the library, the laboratory, and now the cellar. I've examined guest books, mantelpieces, bookshelves, crates, furniture. I've lost my only possession to a stone fireplace. I have NOTHING. The cold is climbing my ribs — that eight-year-old feeling, wearing clothes that were never meant for me. Everyone else is probably finding things. Clara was somewhere, Vincent was somewhere. They're all collecting items and solving puzzles while Reginald Foxworth rummages through empty furniture in a damp cellar like a vagrant. No. Stop. The air vents. They're still there. 'Just big enough for something very small to explore.' I can't fit in them but I can EXAMINE them. Something lives in those vents — the same something that gnawed the wire on the machine upstairs. Something small that redecorates. If I can find what's in those vents — or find the creature — maybe there's something useful. But the distrust is growing. Hartwell and the Brixton Boys are RIGHT HERE watching me examine everything and find nothing. They're watching me fail. My spine is screaming for a win, something I can narrate, something I can point to. The air vents. Last thing in this room. Then I need to change strategy entirely — maybe steal from whoever HAS found something.

desc: I am wagering a family fortune that does not exist on a theory I invented three seconds ago. But the air vents are the only thing left in this cellar I haven't examined, and something — SOMETHING — gnawed through that wire upstairs and decorated this cellar like a tiny interior designer. Whatever is living in these walls might have collected valuables. It's what I would do, if I were small enough to fit in a vent. Which, given how tonight is going, I rather wish I were.

desc: Reginald Foxworth examined the air-vents.
Alone in the library. The mantelpiece watches me pass with its riddle — I know your answer, old friend. A map. But I need your key first, and the key is somewhere I haven't looked yet.
thinking: I'm alone in the library. That's... unusual. The chest tightens slightly — not fear, just the absence of that settling warmth. I'm used to people being near. The room feels bigger without anyone in it, the dust thicker, the mantelpiece staring at me with its riddle like it's waiting for me to do something. I know the answer — a map — and I know it needs a fake medal. But I don't have one. I'm just passing through on my way to the kitchen. Keep moving, Clara. The entrance hall is one room away, and the kitchen is beyond that. Don't stop. The books are still upside down, the chairs still dusty, the inscription still carved. Everything waiting. I'll come back when I have what this room needs.

desc: Clara Bellingham walked into the entrance-hall.

The Brixton Boys: *stops dead in the doorway, eyes flicking between Marsh and the empty space where Clara should be* Where's Clara? *voice sharper than intended* She was just down in the cellar wiv us — well, she was — and now she's... *trails off, staring at Marsh* You been up 'ere the whole time, Marsh? Just... standin' about? In a laboratory? Wiv bubbling chemicals and a machine that could take someone's arm off?
thinking:
Back in the laboratory. Marsh is here. James is here. Clara is NOT here. Again.

Marsh. Right there. Standing in the laboratory like he owns the place. And Clara's gone — slipped off while I was downstairs poking at furniture. My neck is on fire. The prickling is so strong it's almost a burn. Marsh is HERE and Clara is NOT HERE and that means either she went to the library on her own, or... no. Don't think the worst. Not yet.

But look at him. Just standing there. What's he been doing while I was in the cellar? Was he down there before? Did he come up while I went down? Is he always one room ahead of me, one step to the side, always just out of the picture when things happen?

James is here though. Solid James. The warmth in my chest. Shoulders beside mine. He heard what I said earlier about Marsh — I think he heard. Maybe now he can see it too. The man's just... standing in a room full of dangerous equipment, calm as a Sunday morning. Who's calm in a room like this?

Clara must be in the library. That's the only other exit from here. I need to go through there. But if I leave, Marsh stays here with the machine, the tools, the lab equipment. Do I leave James to watch him? Or do I drag everyone with me?

No — stay. Just for a moment. Watch Marsh. See what he does when he thinks nobody's paying attention. That's how you catch people — not in what they do, but in what they do when they think the watching's stopped.

desc: Watch 'is face. Watch 'is hands. When you ask a question and a man's got nuffin' to hide, his body stays still. When he's lying, something moves — a finger, an eye, a shift of weight. The streets taught me that before I could read a book. Let's see what Marsh does when Danny asks a direct question.

desc: James Hartwell: Hold on — the workbench. I've been so fixated on the missing wrench that I've overlooked what's actually here. Tools, it says — but which tools? A man who builds bridges knows that you don't need the perfect tool, you need the right one. Let me take a proper look at what we're working with.
thinking:
Back in the laboratory. Marsh is here. The Brixton Boys are here. Clara is not. The proximity_seek is pulling hard — where is she? Library? Entrance hall? Kitchen?

My jaw locks when I see Marsh. The proving-worth drive fires — shoulders squaring, fingers curling into my palms. He's just standing there. He hasn't done anything. Give the man the benefit of the doubt.

But I need to move. I've been circling these rooms — laboratory, cellar, laboratory — and accomplishing nothing. The kitchen is my target. Through the library, through the entrance hall, to the kitchen. Copper pots, a wood-burning stove, a preparation table. Kitchens have things you can take. Utensils, wire, tools.

Wait. The workbench. I looked at it but I haven't tried to LOOK at it closely, or TAKE anything from it. It says 'covered in tools — but no wrench.' Tools. There are tools on it. I've been so focused on what's missing — the wrench — that I haven't tried to take what's there. Could I take a tool from the workbench? A screwdriver, pliers, anything?

No — the workbench isn't listed as something I can TAKE or EXAMINE. It's just described. The interactive objects are the crates, the machine, and the workbench — but the workbench has no action tags. No EXAMINE, no TAKE.

The library then. Through to the entrance hall. To the kitchen. That's the path. Stop circling. Move forward.

Actually — I should try LOOKing at the workbench. LOOK can target any object, even ones without explicit action tags. Maybe a closer look reveals something I can take — a specific tool, a piece of wire, something useful.

desc: It's the simplest mistake an engineer can make — cataloguing what's absent instead of inventorying what's present. The workbench has been sitting there this whole time, covered in tools he hasn't bothered to identify because his eye went straight to the gap. His father would have looked at what was there first. His father always looked at what was there first.

thinking: Alone again. Everyone left while I was peering into air vents like a fool. The vents are too small for me — 'just big enough for something very small.' I can't reach in, can't explore them, can't get whatever's inside. The cellar has given me nothing. The air vents mock me. The furniture mocks me. The whole manor mocks me. I'm standing in a damp cellar with empty pockets, empty hands, and a growing coldness in my ribs that I recognise from a long time ago. The plate is empty. Everyone else has already eaten. Stop. STOP. Think like a Foxworth. What do I actually know? The machine upstairs needs three operators and a fixed wire. The wire was gnawed — by something that lives in these vents. The workbench has tools but no wrench. I've been running from room to room examining things and finding nothing because I've been working ALONE. That's the wrong scheme. The right scheme is to find out what the OTHERS have found and take it from them. Steal. That's an action I can perform. STEAL from a character. I need to go back to where people are and find out who's carrying what. The entrance hall, the kitchen — places I haven't been to yet. The kitchen! I never actually went there. I told the Brixton Boys to go there but I never went myself. There could be things there. And there are rooms I haven't explored at all. Back up through the laboratory. Find people. Find what they're carrying. Then — take it. The youngest of four learned to take things when nobody was looking. Time to remember that lesson.

desc: I have found absolutely nothing. Not a single, solitary thing. Four rooms, empty hands, and a growing suspicion that I've been outplayed by everyone in this manor including whatever small creature has been redecorating the cellar. New plan: stop examining things like an honest worker and start doing what Reginald Foxworth does best — finding out what other people have and taking it. The kitchen is still unexplored. There must be rooms beyond it. And somewhere in this manor, someone is carrying something valuable. My fingers remember how to make things disappear into pockets. It's time to stop being an explorer and start being a thief.

The workbench has tools but no wrench. I've been running from room to room examining things and finding nothing because I've been working ALONE. That's the wrong scheme. The right scheme is to find out what the OTHERS have found and take it from them. Steal. That's an action I can perform. STEAL from a character. I need to go back to where people are and find out who's carrying what. The entrance hall, the kitchen — places I haven't been to yet. The kitchen! I never actually went there. I told the Brixton Boys to go there but I never went myself. There could be things there. And there are rooms I haven't explored at all. Back up through the laboratory. Find people. Find what they're carrying. Then — take it. The youngest of four learned to take things when nobody was looking. Time to remember that lesson.

I believe she may have headed back toward the library. You might want to check on her — those bookshelves are rather top-heavy, and I'd hate for one to topple. Now, I really must pop through to check on the kitchen. The old master's pantry needs an inventory, and I've been putting it off all afternoon. Do excuse me, gentlemen!

But wait — stop, Danny. Think. I've been chasing ghosts through this house for an hour. Room to room, always one step behind. That's not protecting, that's panicking. A panicked dog runs in circles. A guard dog picks a spot and holds it.

A locked cabinet with a brass lock — Grandmother's attic all over again, except this time I need a brass key, not every key in the house. And would you look at that — rat poison, up on the high shelf. Now, I am not generally in the business of poisoning anything, but there is a little critter somewhere in this house that has been chewing through wires and making a nuisance of itself in the laboratory. I think I had better hold onto this, just in case.
thinking: Oh! Oh my. Now THIS is a room with things happening. Three items — a stove that's still warm (someone was here recently!), a locked cabinet that needs a brass key, and — rat poison. On a high shelf. Rat poison. The wire in the laboratory was gnawed through. By a rat. And here's rat poison. That connects. But do I want rat poison? The something-small that travels through the air vents and gnaws wires — is it a pest to be dealt with, or is it part of the puzzle? And that cabinet — another lock, another key I don't have. The brass key. Where is a brass key in this house? The laboratory had brass instruments. The machine was brass-and-copper. But I didn't find a key there. The stove is still warm. That's the most telling detail — someone was cooking, or at least warming themselves, very recently. This house is not as abandoned as it looks. Between the cheerful cellar decorations and the warm stove, someone is living here. Mr Pemberton, the estate manager? My belief says he's helpful and charming. Maybe he's the one keeping house. The stove is examinable — let me look at it. It might have something inside it or near it. But the rat poison... it's TAKE-able. My first item! Part of me recoils — poison is ugly, poison hurts things — but it's the first thing in this entire mansion I can actually pick up. And there's a rat problem that's blocking the machine. Practical Clara says take it. Soft Clara says... well, soft Clara will figure out if it's needed later. Take it for now.

My body is doing that thing — the drives colliding. Hands wanting to reach for her, legs wanting to position, jaw locking at the sight of Marsh. The heat behind my sternum and the weight on my shoulders are pulling in different directions and I'm standing in the middle of it, fingers curling and uncurling, caught between reaching out and building something.

Clara must be in the entrance hall. Or the kitchen. She's the only person not accounted for — wait, Foxworth isn't here either. Clara and Foxworth, somewhere together? That's... actually fine. Focus. The kitchen. Through the entrance hall. I'm passing through. Don't get distracted by the mantelpiece again — I know what it needs and I don't have it. Don't examine the bookshelves again. Don't stop.

But Marsh is right here. And there's something I haven't tried. I could talk to him. The man makes my neck prickle but I've been avoiding him rather than engaging. Give the man the benefit of the doubt — that's the rule. Maybe if I talked to him, I'd understand what it is about him that sets me off. Or maybe he knows something about the manor that I don't. He's been exploring too.

No. Kitchen first. Items first. Be useful first. Talk later. James Hartwell proves his worth through his hands, not his conversation. Move.

Where'd 'e get a bleedin' MEDAL from? *rushes toward the mantelpiece, trips over the corner of a reading chair and crashes into the stonework shoulder-first* OW! And now Foxworth — quiet, always-there Foxworth — has gone and used it on the mantelpiece while I wasn't looking?

desc: The game wants me to poison the tea. I can feel it — the rat poison in my pocket, the cups laid out so neatly. But Clara Bellingham does not poison tea. Not today. Not ever. There is another use for this poison, and it involves a wire-chewing rat, not a tea party.

My stomach drops — not the puzzle-fizz, not the adventure-lightness, but something cold and wrong. Why would I poison tea meant for my friends? For anyone? That is not who I am. That is not who Clara Bellingham is. I feel sick thinking about it — the same sick I felt when my parents argued, that tightness that wouldn't let me eat. Someone put this poison on a shelf in the kitchen, and someone set tea for everyone in the ballroom, and the game is connecting those two things and I do not like what it's suggesting. No. Absolutely not. I will examine this tea service to learn more about it, but I will not — I will never — poison tea meant for people. Even if the game lets me. Even if it's a puzzle solution. There has to be another way. The rat poison is for the rat. For the wire. For the machine. Not for people's tea. My hands are shaking slightly and I don't like it. Let me look at this tea service and understand what it is before I decide anything.

desc: Clara Bellingham examined the tea-service.

The Brixton Boys: *voice echoing in the empty library* Oh, for the love of — EVERYONE'S GONE! *spins around, looking at both exits* I said 'plant yourself, Danny.' I said 'hold the crossroads.' And what 'appened? Everyone walked off and left me guardin' an EMPTY ROOM! *kicks a dust ball across the floor* Brilliant strategy, that. Top marks. The great Danny of Brixton, guardin' a pile of books what nobody wants to read! *heads for the door at speed, catching his hip on the corner of a reading chair* OOF! — that'll bruise in the mornin'!
thinking:
Alone. Completely alone. The library is empty. Every single person has gone — Clara, James, Marsh, Foxworth. All of them. I'm standing in an empty room talking to dust and old books.

My chest is crushing. That gravitational pull — it's yanking in every direction at once because I don't know where ANY of them are. Clara could be anywhere. With anyone. The weight behind my ribs that never lifts is now a stone, heavy and cold, because the people it orients toward have vanished.

I said I'd hold the crossroads. I said I'd plant myself and let them come to me. And they didn't come. Nobody came. I'm standing in an empty library like a bouncer at a party where everyone's left.

This was wrong. This was the wrong play. Standing still doesn't work when the people you're protecting are moving. You can't guard a door nobody walks through.

Entrance hall. That's the real hub — it connects to the kitchen AND the library. If Clara's anywhere accessible, she's there, or she passed through there. And the chandelier — that precarious chandelier hanging over the foyer. If Clara's standing under it and someone bumps the wrong thing...

Move. NOW. Stop thinking, stop watching, stop waiting. Get to the entrance hall. Find Clara. Be where she is. That's all that matters. That's all that's EVER mattered.

Where else would I be?

desc: Alone. The word sits in me like a stone in cold water. I was eight and I sat outside that door all night because leaving felt like something breaking. Right now, standing in this empty room, everything's breaking. Clara's out there. She's out there and I'm in HERE. Where else would I be? Anywhere but here. Anywhere she is.

desc: The Brixton Boys walked into the entrance-hall.

James Hartwell: Foxworth — good, you're here. I've been making a thorough survey of this manor and I could use a fellow man of reason. Here's what I've pieced together so far: there's a riddle on the library mantelpiece — the answer is a map — but it needs a fake medal to activate. There's a machine in the laboratory that requires three operators and a wire repair. Something small is living in the walls, travelling through the air vents, and it's been keeping this stove warm and redecorating the cellar. And now there's a locked cabinet here with a brass lock. Have you come across a brass key anywhere in your travels? Or anything else of use? James Hartwell believes in pooling resources — two minds are better than one, especially when one of those minds has been examining every blessed surface in this manor without finding a single thing he can put in his pocket.
thinking:
Clara is gone again. She was here — I spoke to her, I asked if she was cold, I examined the stove — and she left. Foxworth is here instead. The rib-tightening, the gap where the wall should have been. I keep losing her. I keep arriving in rooms just as she leaves, or she slips away while I'm examining something. I'm chasing her through this manor like a lovesick ghost and she keeps dissolving around corners.

The stove. Still warm. Cast iron. That's all the examine gave me. Another dead description. I am beginning to wonder if I'm approaching this entire manor wrong. I keep examining things and getting the same descriptions back. No hidden items, no secret compartments, no revelations.

The locked cabinet. Brass lock. Requires a brass-key. I don't have a brass key. Where would a brass key be? Not in any room I've searched — and I've searched them all except the ballroom. The ballroom — cracked marble floor, dusty curtains, a dining table set for tea. That's new territory.

But Foxworth is here. I haven't really talked to anyone. I've been so focused on examining objects and chasing Clara that I haven't engaged with any of the other characters. Maybe Foxworth knows something. Maybe he's found something. Maybe he has the brass key or knows where one is. Cooperation — that's what Father showed me on the country road. Two men fixing each other's cars. You don't have to do everything alone.

Talk to Foxworth. Ask what he's found. Share what I know. Two men comparing notes might crack this manor open faster than one man examining every surface alone.

desc: He's embarrassed. Not visibly — James Hartwell doesn't do visible embarrassment — but somewhere beneath the earnest briefing there's a man admitting he's been thorough to the point of futility. His father would have asked for help three rooms ago. His father would have shaken Foxworth's hand and said 'what have you got?' and meant it without any of this proving-worth nonsense getting in the way. The shoulder-weight lifts half an inch as he says it out loud. Asking for help is not the same as admitting defeat. It's the country road. It's two strangers fixing each other's cars.

desc: Vincent Marsh: Right then! I believe it's high time I put the kettle on. A proper cup of tea — that's what this evening calls for. All this exploring has left everyone rather parched, I'm sure. The kitchen is just through here. Do carry on, gentlemen — I shan't be long!
thinking:
The pull-aside with Reginald is done — he's gone now. The Brixton Boys are here instead. I didn't get visible feedback from the conversation with Reginald, but the pull-aside happened. Whatever intelligence I gathered, I need to act on it.

The Brixton Boys. The ones who watch too closely. My skin prickles around them — the ears sharpening, the peripheral awareness widening. They're the most dangerous observers in this house. Not because they're clever in the way I'm clever, but because they have street instincts. They read people the way I read people — differently, but effectively.

The kitchen. I still haven't been there. It's right here — one move away. I've been circling for turns, pulled aside by conversations and dead-end examinations. Enough. The kitchen is unexplored territory. Copper pots, a wood-burning stove, a preparation table. Kitchens in old houses are treasure troves — drawers, pantries, hiding places. And kitchens are full of things that can be used as weapons, or arranged as accidents.

The Brixton Boys are watching. Let them watch. Pemberton going to the kitchen is the most natural thing in the world — 'Must put the kettle on!' That's exactly what an estate manager would do. It's almost suspiciously normal, which is exactly why it works.

Kitchen. Now. No more delays.

desc: Enough circling. Enough examining empty crates and damp walls and furniture that hides nothing. The kitchen — the one room in this entire house I haven't set foot in — is right there, one doorway away, and I have wasted an unconscionable number of turns NOT going to it. Vincent Marsh does not make the same mistake twice. Tea, he says. TEA. As if the only thing brewing in that kitchen will be Darjeeling. Let us see what the pantry holds — besides, perhaps, the next step in a plan that is long overdue for crystallising.

And this ballroom — gorgeous as it is with that cracked marble floor — only has the one way out. I've been through six rooms now, and I'm starting to think this house has secrets I've been walking right past. Maybe I need to stop examining the furniture and start examining the rooms themselves. There might be hidden doors, secret passages — this is exactly the kind of house that would have them!
thinking:
The ballroom is a dead end — only one exit back to the kitchen. The tea service examined but revealed nothing beyond what I already knew. Silver tea set, cups for everyone. The only interaction is USE with rat-poison, and I am not doing that. I am not poisoning tea that people might drink. That goes against everything I am — everything my body tells me about keeping people safe, about harmony, about the warmth that hums when everyone is okay. The poison is for the rat. Period.

The cellar only connects back to the lab. I've hit both dead ends. Unless there are hidden exits I haven't found... Let me go back and look more carefully. desc: Six rooms. One item. No diamond. But every locked box opens eventually — you just have to find the right key. Or in this case, maybe the right wall to push on.

Reginald Foxworth: A locked cabinet! Well, well, well — now we're getting somewhere! I recognise this type of brass lock immediately — Foxworth and Sons manufactured these in 1887. Finest locks in the Empire. And I happen to know that the keys were always hidden near a heat source — standard Victorian security practice. The stove, Hartwell! The key will be near the stove! I'll check — you guard the cabinet. Don't let ANYONE near it. This is OUR find.
thinking: The kitchen. NEW ground. And immediately my gut clenches hard — a LOCKED CABINET with a BRASS LOCK. 'Requires: brass-key.' A locked cabinet. Something worth locking away. My ribs are tightening around it already, the hollow pulling downward, my whole torso leaning forward before I've decided to move. But I don't have a brass key. I don't have ANYTHING. The stove is still warm — someone's been here recently, or something has been burning. EXAMINE-able. And there's a ballroom beyond — cracked marble floor, dusty curtains, a dining table set for tea. More rooms. More possibilities. But this cabinet — this CABINET. It's the first locked thing I've found in the whole manor. Locked means valuable. Locked means someone didn't want it found easily. The brass key must be somewhere in this house. Where? I've been through the entrance hall, library, laboratory, cellar — did I miss it? Was it in the crates? On the workbench? Hidden in the furniture? Or is it in a room I haven't seen yet — the ballroom? Hartwell is here. He might have the key. He might know where it is. But first — the stove. It's warm. Something might be inside it, behind it, under it. A key hidden near the warmth. Examine the stove. If there's nothing, try the ballroom. The cabinet is the target now. Everything else is just steps toward opening it.

desc: Foxworth and Sons has never manufactured so much as a doorstop, let alone a brass lock. But THERE — a locked cabinet! The first genuinely promising thing I've seen all evening! My hands are shaking. My ribs are so tight I can barely breathe. Something is IN that cabinet, something worth locking away, and Reginald Foxworth is going to find the key and open it before anyone else even knows it exists. The stove is warm — someone or something has been using it. If the key isn't there, it's in the ballroom. But it EXISTS, and knowing it exists is already more than I had five seconds ago.

desc: Reginald Foxworth examined the stove.

The Brixton Boys: *stands in the empty foyer, breathing hard, looking up at the chandelier swaying slightly in a draft no one can feel* You know what, I'm startin' to fink this 'ouse is laughin' at me. *voice cracks slightly, then hardens* Every room I walk into — empty. Every person I try to find — gone. It's like someone's shufflin' the deck while I'm still tryin' to pick a card. *looks toward the kitchen door* Kitchen. That's the one place I ain't been yet. And if Clara ain't in there... *swallows hard* ...if she ain't in there, then I don't know where she is. And Danny not knowin' where Clara is — that's not a situation, that's a CATASTROPHE.
thinking:
Empty. The entrance hall is empty. Nobody. Not Clara, not James, not Marsh, not Foxworth. Just me, the wobbly coat rack, and that chandelier hanging above like a guillotine waiting for a neck.

I'm alone in this house. No — I'm not alone in this house. They're all HERE, somewhere, in these rooms, moving through doors I'm not watching, turning corners I can't see. But I'm alone in THIS room and I've been alone in the LAST room and my chest is a black hole, collapsing inward, pulling toward people who aren't here.

The kitchen. That's the only place I haven't been. Kitchen connects to here. Everyone I know is somewhere in this house and the kitchen is the one room I haven't checked. Clara could be there. Could've been there the whole time while I was running circles through the library and the lab and the cellar.

But I need to stop. Just for one second, I need to stop and breathe and THINK. I've been chasing. Running room to room. And every time I enter a room, it empties. Like the house itself is moving people around, keeping them just out of reach. Is that what this is? Is someone orchestrating this? Marsh? Foxworth? The house?

No, Danny. Houses don't move people. People move people. Someone is making sure I can't find Clara. Someone is keeping me separated from her.

The kitchen. Last room. Only room left. Go.

desc: I promised 'er father. On 'is deathbed I promised. And right now I can't even find 'er in a house with five rooms. What kind of protector loses the person 'e's protectin'? The kind who took the beating for 'is mate's shoes but couldn't stop the next one. The kind who sat outside the door all night but couldn't stop the sickness. I show up. I always show up. But sometimes showin' up ain't enough.

Between the warm stove, the redecorated cellar, and a tea service, I'd say our mysterious host is rather more hospitable than the cobwebs suggest. Gentlemen, if you'll excuse me — James Hartwell has one more room to investigate, and he does not rest until every corner has been accounted for.

Clara is gone again. Marsh is here now — appeared while I was waiting, talking to Foxworth. My neck burns. Clara is somewhere in this manor without me, and Marsh was just... where? With her? Did they pass each other? Did he follow her?

Give the man the benefit of the doubt. Father would.

But my body doesn't listen to Father right now. The jaw is locked. Shoulders squared. Fingers pressing into palms.

thinking:

desc: James Hartwell: Good God — a tea service. Set for everyone, silver cups, the works. In an abandoned manor where something lives in the walls and someone has been keeping house. And unless I'm very much mistaken, this tea is meant to be drunk. Well — not before James Hartwell has examined every last cup. Nobody — and I mean nobody — touches this tea until I've confirmed it's safe. Not Clara, not Foxworth, not even the Brixton Boys. A gentleman tastes the wine before he lets it be served, and James Hartwell does not let anything past him that could cause harm to the people under his protection.
thinking:

And it can be used with rat-poison.

The protection drive slams into my legs so hard I nearly stagger. My whole body repositions toward the tea service, between it and the doorway, as if I could physically block the danger.

Who would poison tea? Why is this even a possibility? The creature in the walls — it's not a rat, I've established that. Something that redecorates and keeps stoves warm. But rat poison exists somewhere in this manor, and someone could put it in the tea.

Marsh. The prickle. The thing I can't prove. Is this what my neck has been trying to tell me? No — give the man the benefit of the doubt. Anyone could find rat poison. The Brixton Boys are rough. Even Foxworth — no, I don't suspect Foxworth.

The tea service. I need to examine it. I need to know if it's already been tampered with. And if it hasn't — I need to make sure it stays that way. Nobody drinks from this until James Hartwell has verified it's safe. Nobody. Especially not Clara.

James Hartwell stands between the danger and the person. That's what the legs do. That's what the neck does. That's what he was built for.
