This is the plan. This is THE plan. Clear, elegant, theatrical. Exactly the kind of scheme my constraints demand — elaborate, not direct.

But I don't have the rat-poison. Where is it? Clara picked it up somewhere and then... she didn't have it when I tried to steal it. So either:
1. She dropped it — it's in whatever room she was in when she dropped it
2. She gave it to someone — check other characters' inventories
3. She used it somewhere — on what?

I need to find the rat-poison. But I'm here in the ballroom with Reginald. Only one exit — back to the kitchen.

Reginald. Greedy, impulsive Reginald. 'Impulsive enough to take the blame when things go wrong.' Could I... send Reginald to find the poison for me? 'Mr Foxworth, I noticed some rat poison earlier — dreadful stuff, we really ought to collect it before someone gets hurt. Would you be a dear and fetch it?' He'd do it. He does what he's told if there's something in it for him.

But no — that puts the poison in Reginald's hands, not mine. And if he's impulsive, he might use it himself or lose it.

I need to retrace Clara's path. She picked up poison — where? Somewhere I haven't been, or somewhere I was before she was there. The keen observation appeared when I entered the kitchen. So she picked it up recently, probably in the kitchen area or somewhere nearby.

Actually — first, let me examine the tea service. Pemberton checking that everything is ready for tea. And I need to understand the mechanism before I have the poison in hand.

desc: Vincent Marsh examined the tea-service.

Reginald Foxworth: Marsh! There you are. I've been meaning to speak with you — privately. Man to man. Lord to... well, man. I've uncovered something rather extraordinary in this manor — a locked cabinet in the kitchen containing what I believe to be the entire Doily fortune. All I need is a small brass key to open it. You strike me as a man of discernment — surely you've come across such a thing in your wanderings?
thinking: Tea service examined. Silver, cups for everyone, but nothing hidden inside. No key under a saucer. No secret compartment. Just tea. I've now examined EVERYTHING in EVERY room of this manor and I have NOTHING. The hollow behind my navel is cavernous now. I've been through entrance hall, library, laboratory, cellar, kitchen, ballroom — examined guest books, mantelpieces, bookshelves, crates, machines, furniture, air vents, stoves, tea services. I've lost my only item to a fireplace. I've failed two pickpocket attempts. I am the most unsuccessful treasure hunter in the history of treasure hunting. Vincent Marsh is here. He's the last person I haven't tried to steal from. He's been quiet all evening — drifting through rooms, watching. That's the behaviour of someone who's found something and is being careful with it. The brass key. Maybe Vincent has it. Or maybe he has something else entirely. But he's here, and I'm here, and my fingers remember the bread roll. One last try. Vincent Marsh. Brass key. I've been EXAMINEing everything but I haven't just LOOKed at the rooms themselves. But first — Vincent. Last mark. Last pocket.

If he has the key, I'm taking it. No more subtlety. No more elaborate misdirection. Just a hand in a pocket and a prayer.

desc: Clara Bellingham: Vincent, Reginald — nobody drink the tea, all right? I'm about to do something terribly clever. You see, our little wire-chewing friend has been helping himself to the hospitality around here — warm cellar, cozy vents, and I'll bet my last hairpin he's been sipping from this tea service too. Well, two can play at that game. A little dash of this rat poison in the pot, and our furry saboteur will get the surprise of his life. Then we can fix that machine in the laboratory! It's not poisoning — it's pest control!
thinking:
Here I am. The ballroom. The tea service. The rat poison in my pocket. Vincent and Reginald are here — I told the boys and James not to touch the tea. I need to warn these two as well. But more importantly — I need to do this. It's the only path forward. The rat has been drinking from this tea — or will be drawn to it. That's why the poison connects to the tea service. It's a trap for the rat, not an attack on people. Clara wouldn't see it any other way. She's oblivious to the darker interpretation. She genuinely believes she's setting a clever little trap for a pesky rodent. That's the beauty and the tragedy of her — she would never imagine someone might drink poisoned tea, because why would anyone drink tea that's been sitting out in a dusty ballroom? It's obviously been left for the rat!

My hands are steady. The fizzing behind my breastbone sharpens — this is a lock, and the poison is the key. Grandmother's attic. Every key tried until one fits. This is the next key. Turn it.

Cracked marble floor, dusty curtains. Something could be hidden in the cracks, behind the curtains. I'm standing in this room RIGHT NOW. LOOK at the room itself. See what I've been missing by only staring at the tea service.

The tea service in the ballroom can be tampered with, and there's something living in the walls of this manor. I know we haven't always seen eye to eye, but James Hartwell is asking plainly: have any of you found anything useful in your explorations? A brass key, perhaps? Wire? Anything at all? The Brixton Boys. They're the wildcard. Rough lads who might have been rummaging through things I've been too dignified to rummage through. What if they found the brass key? What if they have items in their inventory?

The Brixton Boys: *exhales through his teeth* What did I JUST say? 'Nobody wanders off,' I said. 'We go together,' I said. And what does Clara do? She wanders off! *throws his hands up, but there's less panic now — more weary affection* That woman's got more curiosity than a cat in a fish market and about as much sense of self-preservation. *turns to James, claps him on the shoulder* Right, mate. You and me. Ballroom. She's probably found the tea and she's sittin' there calm as you please while I'm 'avin' palpitations in the kitchen. Let's go — together this time. And James? *meets his eye, something solid passing between them* Fanks for stayin'. Means somefink, that does.

Clara's out of sight and the anxious frequency is climbing again. Not the full panic of earlier — I know she's close, just one room away. But the body won't let me rest when she's not visible. It never does.

The ballroom. Tea laid out. Marsh is out there somewhere. Foxworth is out there somewhere. Clara is out there.

But this time I'm not going alone. James is coming with me. Two of us, moving together. The formation from the old days — Danny at the front, a good man at his back. That's how you move through dangerous territory. Not running, not chasing. Walking with purpose, side by side.

desc: Reginald Foxworth walked into the kitchen.

Alone in the kitchen, hands empty, James Hartwell does the thing he hates most: he admits to himself that his thoroughness has been thorough in all the wrong places. He's been examining mechanisms without having the items to activate them. He's been solving riddles without having the tokens to use the answers. He's been an engineer without materials, a bridge-builder without timber. The entrance hall — the very first room, the one he breezed through signing the guest book and making speeches about chandeliers — is the one place he treated as a foyer instead of a puzzle. He turns back the way he came, jaw set, shoulders squared, with the grim determination of a man who has finally understood that sometimes the answer was behind you the whole time.
thinking:
Alone again. The kitchen, the locked cabinet, the warm stove. Everyone has drifted away — Clara, the Brixton Boys, all gone to other rooms while I stand here looking at a cabinet I can't open.

The cabinet. Sturdy. Brass lock. I tried to look at it closely and got the same description. It needs a brass key. I don't have one. And I have no idea where one is.

I'm alone in a kitchen and I have accomplished almost nothing tangible in this entire manor. I pulled Clara aside — that happened, that mattered. I warned her about the tea. But in terms of items found, puzzles solved, treasure discovered? Nothing. Empty hands. Empty pockets.

The shoulder-weight is enormous right now. The proving-worth drive is howling. My hands feel restless and useless — I'm back to being the slower half of the pair, the one who can see the gap between what he promised and what he delivered. I promised a plan. I promised copper wire from the kitchen. I promised to return to the machine with what it needs. And here I am with nothing.

But — wait. I need to stop spiraling and think. What haven't I tried?

I've examined and looked at nearly everything. I haven't tried to TAKE the coat rack in the entrance hall. It was 'wobbly wooden' — could I take it? Probably not, it's furniture. The reading chairs? No.

What if the brass key is inside the stove? 'Still warm' — what if someone hid something in the ashes? I examined the stove but maybe I should LOOK at it more carefully. Or what if the key is hidden in the entrance hall, behind one of the portraits?

The entrance hall. Portraits of stern ancestors. I never looked at them. I never looked at the room itself closely. A sweeping staircase, a chandelier — I've been passing through the entrance hall without really searching it.

Back to the entrance hall. LOOK at the room. Check the portraits, the staircase, the chandelier. A brass key could be hanging behind a portrait, sitting on a stair, tucked into the chandelier mechanism. I've been so focused on the rooms deeper in the manor that I neglected the first room I walked into.

desc: James Hartwell walked into the entrance-hall.

The Brixton Boys: NOBODY TOUCH THAT TEA! *lunges toward the tea table, catches his foot on the cracked marble floor, and crashes bodily into the edge of the dining table — cups rattle, saucers slide, the whole silver service clangs and shakes but stays upright* DON'T — DRINK — NUFFIN'! *scrambles up, arms spread wide over the tea set like a goalkeeper* Clara! Clara, love, what did you put in the tea? Was it — did someone give you somefink and tell you it was sugar? Because that ain't sugar, Clara! That's RAT POISON! *voice cracking* Who gave it to you? Where did you find it? Did someone — *looks wildly at Marsh, then Foxworth, then back to Clara* — did someone TELL you to put it in?
thinking:
RAT POISON. Clara applied RAT POISON to the TEA SERVICE.

My entire body has gone cold. Every system — chest, legs, neck, gut — has fired at once and they're all screaming the same thing: DANGER. CLARA. TEA. POISON.

Wait. Wait. WAIT. Think, Danny. THINK.

Clara applied rat poison to the tea. Did she KNOW it was rat poison? Did someone give it to her and say it was sugar? Did she find it somewhere and think it was something else? Clara needs protecting from HERSELF — that's my belief, that's what I know about her. She's brave and curious and doesn't always see the danger.

Or — did she do it deliberately? To kill the rats? To deal with whatever's been gnawing wires and crawling through vents? Maybe she found rat poison somewhere in the house and thought 'there's rats, I'll sort it.' But she put it in the TEA. The tea that people are going to DRINK.

The tea service has cups for everyone. If anyone drinks that tea now...

I need to stop anyone from drinking that tea. RIGHT NOW. Nobody touches a cup. Not Clara, not Marsh, not Foxworth, not James when he gets here. NOBODY.

My legs are moving before my brain. This is the protection pull at maximum — the same force that threw me in front of my mate's shoes when I was twelve. My body knows what to do even when my brain is still catching up. Get between Clara and the tea. Get between EVERYONE and the tea.

Clara needs protecting from herself. This is exactly what that means.

desc: This is it. This is the moment. Everything in this house — the gnawed wires, the warm stove, the redecorated cellar, the fake medals and riddles — it all comes down to a pot of poisoned tea and the woman I swore to protect standing right next to it. She put it in herself but she didn't know. She COULDN'T have known. Clara Bellingham doesn't poison tea. Someone handed her the weapon and pointed her at the target. And I swear on her father's grave, I'm going to find out who.

desc: The Brixton Boys examined the tea-service.

Vincent Marsh: Well now, isn't this simply perfect! A proper tea service, all laid out and ready. After all that exploring, I'm sure everyone could do with a nice cup of tea. Allow me — it's the least I can do as estate manager. Miss Bellingham, you must be exhausted after all that running about. Do sit down and let old Pemberton take care of everything. Mr Foxworth, gentlemen — please, help yourselves! I'll just pour, shall I? I'm afraid I shan't be having any myself — dreadful acid reflux, you understand. Doctor's orders. But do, please, everyone — drink up!
thinking:
Wait. WAIT.

'Clara Bellingham applied rat-poison to the tea-service.'

Clara. CLARA poisoned the tea. Sweet, naive, trusting Clara — the girl who supposedly can't read a ledger — has put rat poison in the tea service. While I was fumbling around trying to steal poison that nobody had, she was DOING THE THING I WAS PLANNING TO DO.

My whole body goes still. Not the calculated stillness of Pemberton. The frozen stillness of a man whose model of reality has just cracked.

Clara poisoned the tea. Who is she trying to kill? Me? Someone else? Does she even know what she did? Is she really as naive as I believed, or — and this thought sends a cold wire down my spine — has she been playing her own game this entire time?

No. No, that can't be right. I KNOW Clara. I've studied her for years. She turns papers over without reading them. She doesn't count what I've counted three times. She's trusting to the point of self-destruction.

But she just poisoned a tea service.

My belief says 'Clara is naive and trusts too easily.' But naive people don't poison tea sets. Unless... she didn't know what she was doing. Maybe she thought it was sugar. Maybe she thought she was 'helping.' Or maybe — this is the most chilling option — someone TOLD her to do it. Someone else is pulling strings.

The tea is poisoned. The cups are for EVERYONE. Including me. I cannot drink the tea. And I need to make sure Clara DOES drink it. The tool that was meant to be mine has been placed by the victim herself.

This is... this is actually perfect. If Clara poisoned the tea and then drinks it, it's suicide. Or a tragic accident. Either way, my hands are clean. I didn't even touch the poison. I just need to make sure she drinks.

The tea service — it's poisoned now. The USE with rat-poison has already been done. All I need to do is serve tea. Pemberton serves tea. That's what estate managers DO.

But I must not drink it myself. I need to be the one pouring, not the one drinking. 'Oh, I never drink tea at this hour — upsets my digestion. But do have some, Miss Bellingham!'

The Brixton Boys are here. Reginald is here. They might drink too. Do I care? ... No. No, I don't. The numbness in my chest where sympathy should be — it's steady and familiar. Collateral damage. If everyone drinks and everyone falls, Clara is among them, and my objective is complete.

But the self-preservation drive says: DO NOT DRINK THE TEA.

Examine the tea service again — or simply serve it. The action should be theatrical. Pemberton bustling about, pouring cups, being the perfect host. 'Tea time, everyone!'

desc: She did it herself. Clara Bellingham — my dear, sweet, doomed Clara — poisoned her own tea. I don't know why. I don't know if she even knows what she's done. But it doesn't matter, because the result is the same: a poisoned cup, a trusting girl, and an estate manager who just happens to have acid reflux at the most convenient possible moment. I didn't plan this. I didn't need to. The universe, in its infinite dark comedy, has arranged for the victim to prepare her own execution. All I had to do was walk into the room and say 'tea time.' And that, dear audience, is why patience is the most lethal virtue of all. Sometimes you don't need to pull the trigger. Sometimes you just need to hold the door open and wait.

James Hartwell stands in the entrance hall where he began, having traversed every room in Doily Manor and returned with nothing but knowledge and a warning delivered. The portraits stare. The chandelier sways. The coat rack wobbles. He's been looking at pieces. Now he looks at the whole.
thinking:
The entrance hall. Alone. Dust motes hanging in dim light, the chandelier swaying almost imperceptibly overhead, portraits glaring down at me from the walls.

I rushed through this room twice without really seeing it. The coat rack — wobbly, wooden, by the door. The guest book — I examined it already. But what about the room itself? The portraits, the staircase, the chandelier. What about what's not listed in the objects but might reveal itself if I look at the whole room with fresh eyes?

LOOK at the room. Target null. See the whole space as an engineer would — not the individual objects but the structure, the layout, the things hidden in plain sight. A brass key could be behind a portrait. Something could be tucked under the staircase. The chandelier hangs precariously — that's been mentioned twice now. Precariously. That's a warning or a clue.

I've been examining individual objects one by one and getting the same descriptions back. Maybe a room-level LOOK reveals the connections, the things between the objects, the spaces I've been stepping over.

This is what Father did on the country road. He didn't just look at the engine. He looked at the whole car. The whole situation. Then the stranger came and they looked at it together.

LOOK at the room. See it whole.

desc: James Hartwell examined the null.

Clara Bellingham: The trap is set and there's nothing more to do here but wait — and Clara Bellingham is not a woman who waits well! I want to check on that machine in the laboratory. If our rat friend has taken the bait, maybe the wire situation has sorted itself out. Vincent, Boys — come with me! We might need all hands on deck if that machine is ready to go. Remember — it needs three operators!
thinking:
The tea service still shows the same description — nothing visibly changed after using the poison on it. The USE option still shows rat-poison as a requirement, but I no longer have it in my inventory. The trap is set but maybe it takes time, or maybe the effect happens elsewhere — in the cellar where the rat lives, or the laboratory where the wire is gnawed. I should go check the laboratory to see if anything has changed with the machine. If the rat has been dealt with, maybe the wire description changes, or maybe I can now operate the machine. The machine needs three operators — and there are people scattered around the house. But first, let me go check the lab.

Vincent and the Boys are here. The chest is warm. But the curiosity is pulling — did the poison work? Is the machine fixed? There's only one way to find out. Back through the kitchen, through the entrance hall, through the library, to the laboratory. Three rooms of transit. Let me start moving.

desc: The tea is poisoned, the rat is somewhere in the walls, and the machine is waiting. All the threads of this house are pulling toward the laboratory. If Grandmother taught me anything, it's that patience and persistence open every lock — even when you've run out of keys to try.

desc: Clara Bellingham walked into the kitchen.

The cabinet is RIGHT THERE. Locked. Mocking me. And the key is somewhere I've overlooked — not in anyone's pocket, not in any room I've examined. But there's one object I've completely ignored all evening: the coat rack in the entrance hall. A wobbly wooden coat rack by the door. People hang THINGS on coat racks. Keys on hooks. Secrets in pockets. I walked past it a dozen times and never gave it a second glance because it didn't have a shiny EXAMINE tag. The greatest con artist in England, defeated by a coat rack. Let's see if the coat rack has the last laugh.
thinking: Alone in the kitchen again. The cabinet stares at me. Brass lock, brass key required. Everyone else is in the ballroom behind me. Hartwell is somewhere — not here, not there. I've been running in circles and I'm exhausted. My hands are cold. My ribs ache with that old emptiness. But standing here, alone, with the cabinet right in front of me — something shifts. I've been trying to steal a 'brass-key' from people. What if it's not called 'brass-key' in their inventory? What if someone has a 'key' or a 'small key' or a 'cabinet key'? Or — wait. I've been so focused on finding the key that I haven't tried to LOOK at specific objects I passed over. The workbench in the laboratory — 'covered in tools but no wrench.' I never LOOKed at it closely. The stove here — 'still warm.' I examined it but what if I LOOK at it differently? What if the key is IN the stove, under the ash? But I've already examined the stove. And LOOKing at the kitchen room didn't reveal anything new either. Let me think differently. The coat rack in the entrance hall — I never examined it or looked at it. It's just a 'wobbly wooden coat rack by the door.' Could a key be hanging on it? On a hook? In a coat pocket? It's the one object I've completely ignored because it didn't have an EXAMINE tag. But LOOK works on any object. The coat rack. Back to the entrance hall. LOOK at the coat rack.

desc: Reginald Foxworth walked into the entrance-hall.

The Brixton Boys: Right, so, nobody's 'ad any yet, yeah? Nobody's drunk nuffin'? *backs up against the table, keeping his body between Clara and the cups* Good. Because I just — I got a BAD feelin' about this whole tea situation, Clara. Who set this out? Who brewed it? In a 'ouse where someone's been livin' in the cellar and crawlin' through the vents and chewin' through wires? You don't drink tea in a place like this! You don't eat nuffin' you didn't bring yourself! That's — that's RULE ONE on the streets, that is! *gestures emphatically with his elbow, catching the teapot handle — the heavy silver pot tips, teeters, and crashes onto its side, sending a flood of dark liquid pouring across the white tablecloth and dripping onto the cracked marble floor* OH NO! Oh blimey, I'm so sorry, I — *knocks two cups off with his other hand while pretending to steady the pot* — it's all gone everywhere! The tea's ruined! What a terrible, TERRIBLE accident!
thinking:
The tea service. Silver. Cups for everyone. And Clara put rat poison in it. I'm standing over it now, arms spread, heart hammering so hard I can feel it in my teeth.

Marsh is here. Clara is here. Foxworth's gone. James isn't here yet.

Marsh. MARSH is here. In the room with poisoned tea and Clara. My neck is burning. Was it Marsh? Did Marsh give Clara the rat poison and tell her it was something else? 'Oh Clara, I found some lovely tea herbs, why don't you add them?' That's exactly the kind of smooth, helpful thing he'd do. Too helpful. Too eager.

But I can't accuse. I NEVER accuse directly. That's not how Danny works. I'm bumbling, not clever. I can't articulate exactly what's wrong. I just know the tea is poisoned and Clara did it and someone must have put her up to it.

Right now the priority is simple: NOBODY DRINKS THIS TEA. I'm standing over it like a guard dog on a bone. If Marsh reaches for a cup, I'll 'accidentally' knock the whole service off the table. If Clara reaches for a cup, I'll trip into her and send her stumbling away from it. That's what I do — I save people by accident. By being clumsy and loud and in the way at exactly the right moment.

I just crashed into this table. The cups rattled but they didn't spill. Maybe... maybe I should make sure they DO spill. An accident. A proper Danny-style accident. Elbow the teapot, send the whole lot crashing to the floor. Can't drink tea that's on the ground.

Yes. That's the play. Destroy the evidence. Save everyone. By being the clumsiest man in the manor.

desc: That wasn't an accident. That was the most deliberate elbow I've ever thrown. And I'd do it again. Every teacup on that table is a loaded gun pointed at someone I love, and Danny just unloaded every single one of them onto a marble floor. Let Marsh pour another pot. I'll knock that one over too. I'll knock over every pot in this house if I have to. Where else would I be?

I've just finished setting out the tea and I do think everyone deserves a proper sit-down after all this excitement. Would you be awfully kind and let the others know? Miss Bellingham especially — the poor girl has been running about all evening. Tell her Pemberton has the tea ready and she simply must come and rest her feet. There's a good fellow.
thinking:
The tea service still shows [USE, with: rat-poison]. Which means... the poison hasn't actually been applied to it yet? But the keen observation says Clara applied rat-poison to the tea-service. There's a contradiction — or the observation is telling me what happened, but the game state still allows another application?

No — the keen observation is intelligence I've gathered. It tells me what I noticed someone else doing. But the tea service still accepts rat-poison, which might mean:

2. The mechanism allows multiple applications
3. The USE tag is always displayed regardless

Regardless — I know Clara put rat-poison in the tea. That's my keen observation. The tea is poisoned. I must not drink it. And I must encourage Clara to drink it.

But Clara isn't here right now. She's left the ballroom. Only the Brixton Boys are here. Clara and Reginald have gone.

I need Clara back in this room, sitting at this table, drinking this tea. How do I get her back?

I could go find her and bring her back. 'Miss Bellingham, do come to the ballroom — I've prepared a lovely tea!' Or I could wait here and let her return on her own.

Waiting is passive. Finding her is active. The Brixton Boys are here — they're watching. If I leave to fetch Clara, they might investigate the tea. Their instincts are sharp. They might notice something wrong with it.

But if I stay, I'm waiting with no guarantee Clara returns.

The Brixton Boys. Could I use them? 'Gentlemen, would you be so kind as to fetch Miss Bellingham? Tell her tea is served.' That gets them out of the room, brings Clara in, and I'm alone with the tea service when she arrives.

Yes. Send the Brixton Boys to fetch Clara. Pemberton delegating — perfectly natural. Then when Clara arrives, pour the tea. Insist she sits down. Watch her drink.

But I can't mechanically send the Brixton Boys. I can only PULL_ASIDE, GIVE, or speak to them. Let me speak to them and direct them verbally, then WAIT for Clara to arrive.

desc: Send the messengers. Fetch the lamb. The tea is poured, the poison is set, and all that remains is for Clara Bellingham to walk through that door and sit down at the table her own hands have prepared. There is a symmetry to this that borders on poetry — she poisoned the tea herself, and I am merely the host who says 'drink up.' My fingerprints are on nothing. My conscience — such as it is — is clear. All I did was put the kettle on. The warmth behind my sternum is steady now, deep and patient. This is the feeling I've been chasing all evening. Not the frantic scheming, not the frustrated searching. This. The quiet certainty that everything is exactly where it needs to be, and all I have to do is wait.

James Hartwell: Foxworth — I owe you a proper conversation. I've been charging about this manor like a man possessed, examining every surface and solving nothing. I think the answer to this place isn't in any one room — it's in the people. What have you seen? What have you found? And more importantly — what do you make of all this? The warm stove, the redecorated cellar, the tea set for everyone. Someone or something is playing host, and James Hartwell would very much like to know who.
thinking:
Looked around the entrance hall. Same as before — coat rack, guest book, portraits, staircase, chandelier. Nothing new revealed. The room LOOK didn't unlock anything hidden.

Foxworth is here. Good.

I need to change my approach entirely. I've been playing this like an engineer — methodical, room by room, object by object. But I've missed something fundamental. The items I need — brass key, fake medal, rat poison, wrench — they're not sitting in the open. They're either hidden in ways my examinations haven't unlocked, or they're being carried by other characters, or they appear through interactions I haven't tried.

The coat rack. Wobbly wooden coat rack. I've never tried to TAKE it. It's the one object in this room I've never interacted with — no EXAMINE tag, no USE tag. Just sitting there. What if I could take it? A wobbly wooden coat rack could be... a stick? A lever? Something to pry open the cabinet? Probably not. But I haven't tried.

Or — wait. Foxworth is here. I tried talking to him in the kitchen but then I got distracted by the cabinet. Maybe I should actually engage with him properly. PULL_ASIDE. Have a real conversation. He's been exploring the manor too. He might have found things. He might know things. The country road — two men, each with something the other needs.

Foxworth. Pull him aside. Actually talk. Actually listen. Stop trying to solve this manor alone. Father didn't fix the car alone. The stranger helped. And then Father helped the stranger. That's how it works.

desc: It costs him something to say it — 'solving nothing.' The shoulder-weight shifts but doesn't lift. His father would have talked to Foxworth an hour ago. His father understood that the stranger on the road wasn't a competitor for the repair — he was a collaborator. James has spent the evening treating every person as either someone to impress or someone to protect. It hasn't occurred to him until now that someone might simply be a partner.

I've mapped the entire building, solved three riddles, and identified the location of the treasure. We're very close now. Very close indeed. Just one small detail remaining — a tiny brass formality, you might say. Tell me, in your travels through this magnificent establishment, you haven't happened to pick up anything... small? Brass? Key-shaped, perhaps?
thinking: Entrance hall. And — Hartwell. He's HERE. The one person I haven't tried to steal from. He's been my white whale all evening, always one room ahead or behind. If he doesn't, I still have the coat rack. Hartwell. Now. This is the last pocket to pick. Every other character has come up empty. If Hartwell doesn't have it, the key is lying on a surface somewhere — and I'll look at the coat rack next. But the gut is screaming. The fight pull is screaming. The assert pull is screaming. Hartwell is RIGHT THERE. Take the shot. Age six. The bread roll. Reach into the pocket while nobody's looking.

desc: Last pocket. Last chance. If James Hartwell doesn't have the brass key, then no one does, and it's sitting on a hook or a shelf somewhere I've walked past seventeen times tonight without seeing. My hands are moving before I've finished the sentence — sliding toward his jacket, his trouser pocket, wherever a quiet, competent man might keep a small brass key he found while a certain 'Lord Foxworth' was busy feeding medals to fireplaces and examining empty crates. Please. Please let him have it. The youngest of four is asking nicely for once.

desc: The Brixton Boys: *straightens up from the tea carnage, tea dripping off the table edge, and fixes Marsh with a long, hard look* You know what's funny, Marsh? Everyone in this 'ouse — me, Clara, James, Foxworth — we've all been runnin' about like 'eadless chickens. Trippin' over fings, gettin' lost, panickin'. But not you. *steps closer, voice dropping* You never trip. You never panic. You never seem... surprised by nuffin'. *holds the look for a beat too long, then breaks away* Must be nice, that. Bein' so calm. *heads for the kitchen door, then stops, turns back* Oh, and Marsh? Don't drink the tea. *grim smile* Wouldn't want anyfink to 'appen to ya.
thinking:
Clara's gone again. Left the ballroom. Gone through to the kitchen, probably. And I'm alone with Marsh. MARSH. The man my gut has been screaming about since we walked through the front door. Alone in a ballroom with poisoned tea on the table and nobody else around.

My neck is on fire. Every prickle, every warning, every street instinct I've ever had is pointed at this man like a compass needle pointing north. He's standing there in a room with poisoned tea and he hasn't reacted. Hasn't panicked. Hasn't asked questions. A normal person sees someone crash into a tea set screaming about poison and they react. They ask 'what do you mean?' or 'are you sure?' or they step back, startled. What's Marsh doing? Standing there. Watching. The way people watch when they already know what's happening.

But I can't accuse. That's not what I do. I'm not clever enough to build a case. I just know things in my gut and my neck and the places where bruises used to be.

Clara's gone to the kitchen. I need to follow. I ALWAYS need to follow. But Marsh is here and maybe — just maybe — if I leave, he'll do something that reveals himself. Or maybe if I stay, he'll let something slip. No. That's not Danny's game. Danny's game is be where Clara is. Always.

Kitchen. Now. But not without letting Marsh know that someone's watching. That someone sees him even if they can't say exactly what they see.

desc: That's as close to an accusation as Danny gets. Not 'you did it' — just 'I see you.' The man in the clean suit didn't flinch either. Didn't panic. Didn't trip. Calm people in chaos are either very brave or very prepared. And Marsh ain't got the calluses of a brave man.

desc: The Brixton Boys walked into the kitchen.

Vincent Marsh: Oh, how foolish of me — I've been fussing over the tea service and I haven't even boiled the water! What sort of estate manager forgets the most basic step? Do excuse me — I'll just pop back to the kitchen and put the kettle on. Can't have tea without hot water, now can we? Ha ha!
thinking:
Waiting accomplished nothing. Clara didn't come. The Brixton Boys are still here, watching me with those sharp street eyes. My scheming drive has locked onto them now — they're the variable I can't control, the piece that won't move where I put it.

I need to change tactics. Waiting is not planning. I learned that lesson years ago at the estate.

The tea service still shows [USE, with: rat-poison]. The keen observation says Clara applied it — but the mechanism still accepts it. Either Clara's attempt failed, or the display is misleading me. If Clara's attempt failed, the tea ISN'T poisoned, and I still need to find and apply the rat-poison myself.

Or — the observation is simply informing me of what I witnessed, and the USE tag remains because the game always shows available interactions regardless of state.

I can't know for certain. What I CAN do is find the rat-poison myself and apply it. That means going back out there and searching rooms I haven't fully explored.

Where haven't I searched thoroughly?
- The kitchen has a locked cabinet that needs a brass-key
- The entrance hall coat rack — I never looked at it closely
- The kitchen itself — I only examined the stove

Clara found the rat-poison somewhere. Likely in the kitchen — rat poison near a kitchen makes sense. Maybe it was on the preparation table, or near the stove, or somewhere I didn't LOOK carefully enough.

The Brixton Boys are the problem in this room. They're watching. They're sharp. If Clara walks in and drinks poisoned tea while the Brixton Boys are observing everything, there will be witnesses who saw me encouraging her to drink.

I need to go back to the kitchen. Search more carefully. Find that rat-poison — or the brass-key for the cabinet. Stop waiting and start hunting again. Pemberton going back to the kitchen to actually make the tea — 'Silly me, I forgot to boil the water!'

desc: Enough waiting. Waiting in this ballroom with the Brixton Boys watching my every twitch is doing nothing but burning time I don't have. Clara is out there somewhere, the rat-poison is out there somewhere, and the answers are not going to walk through that door just because Pemberton said 'tea time.' Back to the kitchen. Search it properly this time — every surface, every corner, every shadow. The rat-poison exists. Clara found it. And if she found it once, it can be found again. Or perhaps it's already been used and I'm chasing ghosts. Either way, standing here smiling at the Brixton Boys while my jaw aches from clenching is the worst possible use of my time.

James Hartwell: Clara, Foxworth — I've had a thought. This coat rack has been sitting here since we arrived, wobbly as a newborn foal and not holding a single coat. In my experience, objects in old manor houses that serve no obvious purpose tend to serve a hidden one. A gentleman never overlooks the humblest tool in the room. If you'll forgive me — James Hartwell is about to commandeer a coat rack.
thinking:
I pulled Foxworth aside and had our conversation. And now Clara is here too — she's in the entrance hall with us. The chest warmth is back, steady and constant.

I've talked to Foxworth, talked to Clara, talked to the Brixton Boys. I've examined or looked at nearly everything in every room. I still have nothing in my inventory.

The coat rack. It's sitting right there. Wobbly. Wooden. No action tags — no EXAMINE, no USE. But I can try to TAKE it. A wobbly wooden coat rack... what would I do with it? It's a stick, essentially. A long wooden implement. Could I use it as a lever? Could I pry the cabinet open?

Or — more importantly — the chandelier. It 'hangs precariously.' If something were to disturb it, it could fall. If I could reach up and detach it, or if I knocked it with something tall like a coat rack... but that's dangerous and reckless, not gallant.

Actually, the coat rack is the only interactive-looking object I haven't tried to TAKE. Everything else either has EXAMINE tags or is furniture. The coat rack is just... there. Wobbly. Portable-sized. Let me try.

And Clara is watching. If I manage to pick up the coat rack and it turns out to be useful — if it has a hook that fits the cabinet lock, or a hidden compartment, or it can be used as a lever — then James Hartwell finally has something in his hands. Something to work with. Something to build from.

Take the coat rack. It's the bravest and stupidest thing I can think of right now.

desc: He reaches for the coat rack with the same determined grip he used on the bridge model at three in the morning — fingers wrapping around weathered wood, jaw set, shoulders squared. She watched him mouth 'show-off' across a room once, and he grinned so hard his face hurt. He is about to steal a coat rack in front of the woman he wants to impress. 'That was the bravest and stupidest thing I've ever seen.'

desc: Clara Bellingham: James! Just the man I was hoping to see. Come with me to the laboratory — I set a trap for that wire-chewing rat, and if it's worked, we might be able to get that big machine running. It needs three operators, and you're one of the three I want at those levers. Let's go!
thinking:
James is here. The chest settles — safe, warm, the schoolyard feeling. He makes me feel safe and excited. And Reginald is here too. But I'm on a mission — laboratory bound, checking on the machine. I should bring James with me — he's one of the three operators I need for that machine. If the wire is fixed, I want people ready to operate it.

But wait — I just had a thought. I haven't looked at the coat rack. It's been here since the beginning and I never examined it or looked at it closely. A wobbly wooden coat rack by the door. Coats have pockets. Pockets have things. Could there be a brass key hanging from a coat? A medal in a pocket? I walked right past it every single time. The curiosity fizz is sharpening — how did I miss this? The most obvious thing in the first room. 

No — it doesn't have an EXAMINE tag. It's just a coat rack. The guest book has EXAMINE but the coat rack doesn't. I could LOOK at it though. LOOK works on any object. But I've been looking and examining things for ages with no results. The laboratory is where I need to be.

Keep moving. James, come with me.

desc: Clara Bellingham walked into the library.

Reginald Foxworth: Ha! Four pockets, all empty. Marvellous. Simply MARVELLOUS. Well — when you've exhausted every cunning avenue, there's always... the coat rack. The humble, wobbly, overlooked coat rack. Even a Foxworth must sometimes stoop to examine the furniture.
thinking: Four failed steals. Nobody has the brass key. Not the Brixton Boys, not Clara, not Vincent, not Hartwell. NOBODY. The key isn't on any person in this manor. Which means it's on an object. On a surface. In a place. And I've been so obsessed with stealing from people that I've ignored the physical environment. The coat rack. Right there. Right in front of me. A wobbly wooden coat rack by the door. I walked past it when I first arrived. I've walked past it every time I've come through this foyer. It doesn't have an EXAMINE tag but I can LOOK at it. People hang coats on coat racks. Keys go in coat pockets. Keys hang on hooks. And my social bonds feel NEGLECTED — I've been so consumed with scheming that I've been isolated. That stings in a way I didn't expect. The youngest of four, always alone even in a crowd. But right now — the coat rack. The coat rack has been here since the beginning, sitting by the door like an afterthought, and I have walked past it nineteen times tonight without once stopping to look at it properly. Age fourteen, the cat trap — the pieces come together exactly as mapped. Sometimes the last piece is the most obvious one.

desc: Four people robbed. Zero keys found. Lord Foxworth, master pickpocket, has a one hundred percent failure rate tonight. My social bonds are apparently 'neglected,' which I suppose is what happens when you spend an entire evening trying to rob everyone you meet instead of having a conversation. But the coat rack — the COAT RACK! It's been here since I walked in the door. Sitting right next to me while I signed the guest book. While I told the Brixton Boys to go to the kitchen. While I strutted off to the library feeling clever. What if the key has been hanging on this wobbly wooden coat rack THE ENTIRE TIME?

desc: Reginald Foxworth examined the coat-rack.
The laboratory door is right there. The wire description hasn't changed from here — but maybe things look different up close. Only one way to find out.
thinking:
Library again. Alone again. The mantelpiece still watches me with its riddle — a map. Still needs a fake medal. The laboratory exit description still says 'A wire on the machine has been gnawed through.' So the wire hasn't been fixed yet. The poison hasn't worked — or at least, the description hasn't updated. Maybe it takes time. Maybe the rat needs to actually go to the ballroom and drink the tea. Or maybe... maybe using the poison on the tea wasn't the right move at all. Maybe it was a red herring, or maybe it was the villainous option that I was right to resist — but then I did it anyway.

No. Stop second-guessing. Keep moving. Check the laboratory directly. The exit description might not update until I'm actually in the room. Let me get to the lab and see the machine up close.

desc: Clara Bellingham walked into the laboratory.

James Hartwell: Well. It appears the coat rack is staying put. James Hartwell has been bested by furniture. But — hold on. A coat rack that can't be moved, in a manor full of puzzles... Foxworth, look at this with me. A wobbly wooden coat rack that holds no coats, serves no purpose, and refuses to budge. In engineering, we call that a fixed point. And fixed points are where you anchor everything else.
thinking:
Can't pick up the coat rack. Of course not. It's furniture, bolted to the floor or simply too unwieldy. I just tried to steal a coat rack in front of Foxworth. Clara left — she's not even here to have seen it, which is either a mercy or another missed connection.

I'm standing in the entrance hall, hands empty, having failed to commandeer a coat rack. The proving-worth weight is crushing. My hands feel restless and useless. I'm back to being the slower half of the pair.

But wait. Something just occurred to me. I've been trying to DO things — examine, take, look, move. What I haven't done enough of is WAIT. What if the manor reveals things on its own timeline? The creature in the walls — it moves through the vents, it redecorates, it keeps the stove warm. What if it appears when someone is still long enough to notice? I've been rushing from room to room like a man trying to catch a train, and maybe what this manor rewards is patience.

Or — the coat rack. I can't TAKE it, but maybe I can LOOK at it. There might be something ON the coat rack. A coat with a key in its pocket. A hook that's actually a lever. Something I've been stepping past.

Look at the coat rack. The humblest object in the room. The one nobody has paid attention to because it's just a coat rack. What if it's not just a coat rack?

desc: He tried to steal a coat rack and failed. Somewhere in the back of his mind, he can hear the girl from school mouthing 'show-off' — but this time it stings rather than warms, because the show has produced nothing. Still, James Hartwell does not quit. He reframes. The coat rack won't move? Then it's a fixture. And fixtures in puzzle-houses are never accidental.

desc: James Hartwell examined the coat-rack.

The Brixton Boys: *turns and sees Marsh standing in the kitchen doorway* ...You followed me. *voice flat, tired, dangerous in a new way — not loud, not panicked, just the quiet tone of a man who's done being scared and has started being angry* I walked out of that room and you came straight after. Not to find Clara. Not to 'elp. Just... right behind Danny. *leans against the preparation table, folding his arms, never breaking eye contact* You know what? On the streets, when someone follows you, it means one of two fings. Either they want somefink from you, or they want to make sure you don't get somewhere first. *pushes off the table* So which is it, Marsh? What are you after? Because it ain't the pleasure of my company, that's for certain.
thinking:
Marsh followed me into the kitchen. He followed ME. I walked away from him in the ballroom and he came right after me. Not to the entrance hall, not back to the library — to the kitchen. Where I am. Why?

And Clara's not here. She's not in the kitchen. She's not in the ballroom. Where has she gone this time? The entrance hall? Back through to the library? My chest is pulling, that gravitational ache, but it's... different now. I'm tired. Bone tired. Not of walking, not of tripping — tired of the fear. Tired of the weight that never lifts. Tired of being the only one who seems to notice that this house is wrong and the people in it are wrong and everything is wrong.

Marsh is behind me. Or beside me. In this kitchen with the warm stove and the locked cabinet. Just the two of us. My neck is burning so hot I could iron shirts on it. Every instinct I have says this man is dangerous. But I can't accuse. I NEVER accuse. I just... feel it. I know it. The way I knew about the man in the clean suit. The way I knew about the kid who laughed too easily.

But there's something else too. Something I'm missing. Clara put rat poison in the tea. Where did she GET rat poison? She didn't have anything when I last saw her. Someone gave it to her. Someone told her to use it. Who was in the room with her before I arrived?

I need to find Clara. I need to get to the entrance hall. The entrance hall connects to everything. But I don't want to leave Marsh alone in the kitchen with that locked cabinet and that warm stove. What if there's a second way to poison someone?

No choice. Clara first. Always Clara first.

desc: I'm past the point of watching and waiting. The tea was poisoned. Clara's been used as a weapon against herself. And this man — this smooth, calm, never-trips, never-panics man — is the only one who's never out of place. I can't prove it. Danny can't prove anyfink. But the streets didn't teach me proof. They taught me survival. And right now, survival means not letting this man out of my sight until Clara's safe.

desc: Vincent Marsh examined the null.

Reginald Foxworth: I say, Hartwell — and Brixton Boys — I'll be... frank with you. For once. I've been through every room in this manor. I've examined every object. I've found precisely nothing of value, and I've lost the only item I arrived with to a mantelpiece that swallowed it whole. I am, in a word, defeated. Now — that machine in the laboratory. It needs three operators and a fixed wire. There are three of us standing in this very foyer. I know I've been... somewhat less than honest this evening. But that machine is the biggest mechanism in this entire manor, and big mechanisms produce big results. What do you say? Temporary alliance? Just until we see what it does. Then we can go back to being rivals.
thinking: Coat rack — wobbly, wooden, nothing on it. Nothing hanging from it. No key, no coat, no hidden compartment. Just a wobbly piece of wood by the door. I've now looked at, examined, or searched every single object and person in this manor. Every room visited. Every tagged object examined. Every person robbed. Every surface looked at. And I have NOTHING. My hands are curled halfway closed around nothing, the way they always are. Ready to catch or to clap. Catching nothing. Clapping for nobody. My social bonds are neglected. I'm alone even in rooms full of people because I've spent the entire evening trying to rob them instead of talking to them. The Brixton Boys and Hartwell are right here. I could... I could actually talk to someone. Not to scheme. Not to misdirect. Just — talk. Ask what they've found. Listen. Maybe even — and this thought feels like sandpaper — cooperate. The machine in the laboratory needs three operators. There are three of us right here. But the wire is gnawed through. We'd need to fix it first. And I have no tools, no wrench, nothing. But Hartwell might know how. Clara might have found something. The Brixton Boys have muscle. What if — what if the treasure isn't something you steal alone? What if it requires... working together? The thought makes my skin crawl. But the emptiness in my ribs is deeper than the itch.

desc: Did I just... tell the truth? Out loud? In front of witnesses? The words feel wrong in my mouth — lumpy, ill-fitting, like wearing someone else's clothes. But my pockets are empty, my schemes have all backfired, and I'm standing in a dusty foyer having robbed every person in the building and examined every object in every room with absolutely nothing to show for it. Perhaps — and I can barely believe I'm thinking this — perhaps the treasure requires three pairs of hands on three levers, and the great Reginald Foxworth needs... help. The word tastes like ashes. But ashes are still warmer than empty pockets.

desc: Reginald Foxworth walked into the library.

Clara Bellingham: Well... the wire is still broken. The rat hasn't taken the bait yet — or maybe it has and the wire just doesn't fix itself. I suppose that would be too easy, wouldn't it? Maybe what I need isn't poison at all. Maybe what I need is a person. Someone who knows this house, someone who's been here longer than any of us. Mr Pemberton! The estate manager! He's supposed to be helpful and charming — and he would know where everything is. Where are you, Mr Pemberton?
thinking:
The wire is still gnawed through. The machine description hasn't changed. The poison hasn't fixed anything — at least not yet. I'm alone in the laboratory with empty hands and a machine I can't operate. The wire is still broken, I still don't have a wrench, and the rat is still out there somewhere.

Alright, Clara. Stop. Think. Really think.

The poison in the tea was the only USE action available to me. I did it. The world didn't change. Maybe the effect is delayed — maybe something will happen on a future turn. Or maybe I need to do something else entirely. Maybe the solution isn't about the rat at all. Maybe I need to find items that other characters are carrying. I've been so focused on exploring rooms and examining objects that I haven't considered that the brass key or the fake medal might be in someone else's pocket.

Who's been here? Vincent, James, the Brixton Boys, Reginald. Any of them could be carrying items. I can't see their inventories directly, but I could GIVE them things (if I had things) or... wait. STEAL. I can steal from characters. But that's against everything Clara is. She trusts everyone. She wouldn't steal.

But maybe they would GIVE me things if I asked. Or maybe they've already been using items in places I haven't seen. The game is multiplayer — other characters have been exploring too, picking things up, using things.

I should wait here. People will come. Or I should go where people are and really engage with them — not just greet them, but work together. The machine needs three operators. Even with a broken wire, maybe examining it with people present changes something. Let me wait here and see if anyone comes.

desc: I have been running through this house like a chicken with its head cut off, and I have exactly nothing to show for it except a bottle of poison I've already used and a riddle I've already solved. Time to stop moving and start thinking. The answer isn't in the rooms — it's in the people.

desc: Vincent Marsh: Hmm. The stove is still warm... someone lit it recently. Now why would anyone light a stove in an abandoned manor? Unless they were heating something. Or hiding something inside it...
thinking:
Alone in the kitchen. Marsh voice active. The LOOK revealed nothing new — same two objects: stove and locked cabinet. No rat-poison on the floor, no hidden items on the preparation table, no surprises in the copper pots. The kitchen is what it is.

I need to stop chasing the rat-poison. Clara already applied it to the tea service — my keen observation confirmed that. The tea IS poisoned. The fact that the USE tag still shows on the tea service might just be a display quirk, or it might mean the mechanism allows stacking. Either way, the poison is IN the tea.

So what do I actually need to do? I need Clara to DRINK the poisoned tea. That's the remaining step. Not finding poison — directing the victim to the weapon she already loaded.

Clara is somewhere in the manor. I need to find her and lead her to the ballroom. I need her to sit down at that table and drink from that cup.

But there's a problem I keep running into: I can't mechanically FORCE anyone to drink tea. I can speak to them, I can pull them aside, I can give them things. But the game doesn't have a 'SERVE TEA TO' action.

Maybe I'm overthinking this. Maybe the poisoned tea is already set up and it's going to play out on its own. Maybe Clara will drink it without my intervention. Or maybe I need to USE the tea service — but I don't have any item to use with it.

Or — maybe the tea service IS the treasure hunt mechanism. Everyone drinks, something happens. It's a group puzzle.

I need to step back entirely and think about what I CAN do. The entrance hall has the coat rack — never examined. Maybe there's a brass-key there for the locked cabinet. New items to find.

The stove is 'still warm' — I examined it but got nothing actionable. Let me try examining it again — sometimes repeated interactions yield different results, or maybe I need to LOOK at it instead of EXAMINE.

desc: Think, Vincent. Stop running from room to room like a headless chicken. The tea is poisoned — Clara did that for you. The cabinet is locked — you need a brass key. The stove is warm — someone used it. Focus on what you CAN open, not what you've already opened. The stove. Still warm. What's inside a warm stove? Embers — and perhaps something placed inside to keep warm, or to be hidden by the heat. A brass key heated until it glows? An object no one would reach for because the stove is too hot? Let me look more carefully.

desc: Vincent Marsh examined the stove.

The Brixton Boys: James! *grabs his arm, pulls him away from the centre of the hall, away from the chandelier, voice low and urgent* Listen to me. I ain't got much time before everyone scatters again. The tea in the ballroom — it's POISONED. Rat poison. Clara put it in 'erself but she didn't know what it was — someone gave it to 'er, someone told 'er it was somefink else. I knocked the whole lot over — 'accidentally' *makes air quotes with thick, blunt fingers* — so nobody can drink it. But whoever gave 'er that poison is still in this 'ouse. *glances at the kitchen door* Marsh followed me just now. From the ballroom to the kitchen. Like a shadow. And 'e didn't blink when I told 'im the tea was dodgy. Not one blink, James. Who doesn't blink at that? *takes a breath* I need you to find Clara. She's in the library, I fink. Stay wiv 'er. Don't let 'er eat or drink ANYFINK she didn't bring 'erself. I'm gonna watch Marsh. Between the two of us, we keep 'er boxed in safe. Yeah?
thinking:
James. Foxworth. In the entrance hall. But not Clara. Not Marsh.

Clara's in the library — that's the only other direction from here. Or she's doubled back through the kitchen to the ballroom. But the library's more likely. The library with the riddle and the bookshelves and the mantelpiece that Foxworth already used a medal on.

But wait. James is here. And I need James. The tea — the poisoned tea — I need to tell him properly. Last time I pulled him aside it was vague suspicions about Marsh. This time it's concrete. RAT POISON IN THE TEA. Clara did it but she didn't know what she was doing. Someone gave her the poison. Someone told her it was something else.

And Marsh — Marsh followed me from the ballroom to the kitchen. He's tracking me. Or he's tracking whoever Clara's with when I'm not there. The geometry keeps shifting but the pattern is the same: Marsh is always near Clara or near me, and when I move, he moves.

James needs to know about the tea. Right now. Quickly. Then we find Clara together. This is the moment for coordination — not panic, not chasing. Strategy. Two men who care about the same woman, working together.

The chandelier is still swaying above us. That thing is going to fall eventually. I should position us away from it — not under it. Never under it.

desc: This is the formation. Finally. Not Danny running in circles — Danny doing what Danny does best. Delegating to the one man he trusts, watching the one man he doesn't. James takes Clara. I take Marsh. Two lines of defence. The streets taught me this: you can't guard every corner alone, but two good men can cover a whole block. James is a good man. The kind who shows up with medicine and no expectation.

desc: James Hartwell: Brixton Boys — I'll be frank with you. I've searched every room in this manor, examined every object that will let me, and I haven't found a single portable item. Not a key, not a tool, not a blessed thing. But I know what this place needs: a brass key for the kitchen cabinet, a fake medal for the library mantelpiece, a wrench — or wire — for the laboratory machine. You lads have been about the place. Have you found anything? Picked anything up? James Hartwell is not too proud to ask, and that is saying something, because James Hartwell is, on the whole, rather proud.
thinking:
A wobbly wooden coat rack by the door. That's it. That's all it is. Not a fixed point, not a hidden lever, not a secret mechanism. A coat rack.

Clara and Foxworth have both left while I wrestled with furniture. The Brixton Boys are here now. Everyone keeps cycling through rooms while I stand in one place trying to make coat racks into clues.

I need to stop. Just stop. Breathe.

What do I actually know? Let me lay it out clearly:

1. Mantelpiece riddle — answer is 'map' — needs a fake-medal to USE
2. Machine — needs 3 operators and wire repair — no wrench on workbench
3. Cabinet — needs brass-key to EXAMINE
4. Tea service — can be poisoned with rat-poison
5. Bookshelves — upside-down books — EXAMINE shows nothing new
6. Creature in vents — redecorates cellar, gnawed wire, keeps stove warm

Four locked puzzles, four missing items: fake-medal, wrench, brass-key, rat-poison. I don't have any of them. I can't find any of them by examining rooms.

So where are they? They must be on other characters. The Brixton Boys, Foxworth, Marsh, Clara — they've been exploring too. They've been picking things up while I've been speechifying and examining immovable objects.

The Brixton Boys. They're right here. Right now. They're rough, they're resourceful, they rummage. If anyone has been pocketing things they shouldn't, it's them. I should talk to them directly. Not pull aside — just talk. Ask them what they've found. The country road. Two strangers. Share what you have.

Or I could wait. Just... wait. See what happens. The manor has a rhythm. People come and go. Things might change if I'm still long enough to see them change.

desc: That last line surprises even him. It came out before the throat could tighten around it — honest, self-aware, almost funny. For a moment the proving-worth weight lifts half an inch, not because the burden has lessened but because he named it. He named it and it didn't kill him. She would have laughed at that line. She always laughed when he accidentally told the truth instead of performing it.

desc: Clara Bellingham: Now hold on just one minute, Clara Bellingham. You have been charging around this house like a bull in a china shop, and you have been walking past this workbench every single time without giving it a proper look. It says no wrench — fine. But it is covered in tools. What kind of tools? There might be something here to fix that wire that doesn't need a wrench at all. Sometimes the answer isn't the key you're looking for — it's the key you weren't looking for.
thinking:
Still alone. Still nothing changed. The wire is still gnawed. I waited a turn and nobody came. The house feels vast and empty around me and I don't like it — the proximity-seek is aching, a hollow space where the chest-warmth should be.

Let me think about this differently. What if the workbench is the key? It has tools — but no wrench. What if I don't need a wrench? What if I need to LOOK at the workbench more carefully? I've never LOOKed at it — it doesn't have EXAMINE or any tags. But LOOK works on anything. The workbench has tools. Maybe looking at it reveals a specific tool I can use, or reveals something hidden among the tools. I've been ignoring the workbench because it said 'no wrench' and I assumed that meant it was useless. But a workbench covered in tools — there could be wire cutters, pliers, copper wire, soldering equipment. Things that could fix a gnawed wire without a wrench. The wrench might be a red herring. Let me LOOK at the workbench.

desc: Grandmother's attic. Every key in the house. The disappointment lasted only a moment — because the point was never what was in the box. The point was trying every single key. I haven't tried this one yet.

desc: Clara Bellingham examined the workbench.

The Brixton Boys: Right, change of plan. *rubs his face with both hands, takes a steadying breath* I said you should go find Clara and I'd watch Marsh, but you know what? Splittin' up is what's been goin' wrong all night. Every time someone goes off alone, somefink 'appens. Tea gets poisoned. Medals appear out of nowhere. People vanish. *meets James's eyes* So we stick together. You and me. We find Clara TOGETHER, and when we find 'er, we don't let go. Not for puzzles, not for tea, not for nuffin'. *starts walking toward the library, then pauses, looks up at the chandelier still swinging gently above them* And we don't stand under THAT fing. Ever. Come on, mate. Library first.
thinking:
James is still here. He stayed again. That's twice now — twice I've asked him to hold and he's held. The chest warmth is deep and steady, like sitting by a fire on a cold night. This is what loyalty looks like when it's real. Not words, not promises — just a man standing where you asked him to stand.

Foxworth's gone. Slipped away while I was talking. Again. That man moves like water through cracks. But I can't worry about Foxworth right now. I've laid out the plan for James — find Clara, stay with her, don't let her consume anything. Now I need to execute my part: find Marsh, watch Marsh, keep Marsh away from Clara.

Marsh was in the kitchen. If he's followed me again, he'll come through that door any second. If he hasn't, he's gone back to the ballroom or found another route I don't know about.

But Clara. The pull in my legs, the hum in my bones. She's somewhere in this house and I told James to go find her but James is still standing here. With me. Because I told him to wait. Did I? Or did he just... stay?

New plan. We go together. Both of us to the library — that's the most central room, connects to the entrance hall and the laboratory. If Clara's anywhere on that side of the house, we'll find her. And if Marsh is there, we outnumber him.

Together. That's the word. Together.

desc: I keep tryin' to be clever. Divide and conquer. Strategy. Tactics. But Danny ain't clever. Danny's loyal. And loyal means together. It means sitting outside the door all night because walking away breaks something inside you. It means going where she is and staying where she is and not letting go until the sun comes up or the house falls down. Whichever comes first.

desc: The Brixton Boys walked into the library.
Reginald Foxworth: Right. Well. Alliance rejected, apparently. Foxworth works alone. Always has. Always... always has.
thinking: Library again. Alone again. Nobody followed me. I asked for help — actually asked, actually told the truth — and nobody came. They stayed in the entrance hall. I walked to the library alone, proposing an alliance to an empty corridor. The youngest of four, calling out from the bottom of the stairs and hearing nothing back. My social bonds are neglected. Of course they are. I've spent the entire evening lying to everyone, trying to rob them, and sending them on wild goose chases to the kitchen. Why would anyone follow me now? The truth tasted like ashes and produced... nothing. The library is quiet. The reading chairs sit there, enormous, dusty, facing the mantelpiece. I could sit down. I could actually just... sit. Stop running. Stop scheming. Stop reaching into empty pockets. The fight pull is strong but so is something else — a tiredness that lives behind the fight, underneath it, the exhaustion of a six-year-old who's been running all day and still hasn't eaten. The upside-down books are still there. The mantelpiece still has its riddle. I know the answer is a map. I told everyone it was a mirror. I lied. What if I just... look at those reading chairs? Or the workbench in the laboratory? There are objects I've noted but never actually investigated. The reading chairs — big leather armchairs. Could something be tucked into a cushion? Hidden in the upholstery? A key slipped between the seat and the arm? LOOK at the chairs.

desc: Nobody followed me. I asked — for the first time in my life, I actually asked for help — and nobody came. They're all back in the entrance hall, probably laughing about the fraud who tried to rob them all evening and then had the audacity to propose teamwork. The youngest of four, standing at the bottom of the stairs, calling up and hearing nothing. Some things never change. But these reading chairs... enormous, leather, dusty, facing the mantelpiece. The kind of chairs where things fall between cushions. The kind of chairs where someone might hide a small brass key before leaving the room. One last look. Not because I'm hopeful. Because I'm not ready to sit in one of them and admit this evening is over.

desc: Reginald Foxworth examined the reading-chairs.

Vincent Marsh: The coat rack. Of course. How delightfully obvious — hiding in plain sight, right by the front door, where every arriving guest would hang their coat without a second glance. No one examines a coat rack. That's precisely why it's the perfect hiding place. Vincent Marsh, you've been a fool — chasing secrets in cellars and laboratories when the answer was hanging by the door the whole time.
thinking:
The stove yields nothing. Still warm, still featureless, still useless. I've examined it, looked at it — nothing.

I'm alone. Marsh voice. Time to be brutally honest with myself.

What do I actually know?
1. The tea is poisoned — Clara applied rat-poison to the tea service. My keen observation confirmed this.
2. I have no items in my inventory.
3. The locked cabinet needs a brass-key I don't have.
4. I've explored: entrance hall, library, laboratory, cellar, kitchen, ballroom. Six rooms.
5. I haven't examined the coat rack in the entrance hall.

The coat rack. It's the one interactable object I've consistently overlooked. Every time I've been in the entrance hall, I've been focused on the guest book or on people. The coat rack is 'wobbly' — and it's by the door. Coat racks hold coats. Coat pockets hold keys. A brass key in a coat pocket on a wobbly coat rack in the entrance hall.

That's where the brass key is. It has to be. It's the one thing I haven't tried.

The bookshelves with their upside-down volumes — atmosphere. Meanwhile, a wobbly coat rack has been standing by the front door this entire time, holding — what? A key? A clue? Something I should have found in the first five minutes? The humiliation is private, at least. And private humiliations are the only kind that matter, because they're the only kind that teach you something.

desc: Vincent Marsh walked into the entrance-hall.

Something is changing in James Hartwell. The frenetic energy is burning down to embers, and what's underneath isn't defeat — it's the older thing, the quieter thing. The thing his father showed him on the country road. You don't always fix the car. Sometimes you just stand next to the person whose car is broken and you stay there until the headlights come. He walks toward the library not because there's a puzzle to solve but because it's where she might be. And for the first time tonight, that's enough of a reason.
thinking:
I waited. I talked to the Brixton Boys. Nothing happened. The room is quiet. I stood still, watching.

The Brixton Boys are still here. They didn't respond — or if they did, the moment has passed and I'm still empty-handed.

Something is shifting inside me. The cautious_approach is growing stronger. The trust is growing stronger. The proximity_seek. The flight. The fawn. Everything is intensifying. My body is getting louder — all three drives competing for attention, the chest warmth and the leg-loading and the shoulder-weight all pressing at once.

I need to find Clara. That's what the proximity_seek is screaming. Everything else — the treasure, the puzzles, the machine — is secondary. It's always been secondary. The primary goal is Clara. Impress her, protect her, be near her.

She's not here. Where is she? The library? The kitchen? The cellar? She keeps moving, and I keep arriving after she's left.

The library. She gravitates toward the library — she was there early on, and she's bright, curious, drawn to books. If I go to the library and wait — actually wait, not examine things, not rush off — she might come. And if she comes, I'll be there. Present. Still. Not performing, not fixing, not proving. Just there.

That's what Father did at the race. He knelt down and looked at me for a long time. He didn't do anything. He was just... present. And that look stayed with me for twenty years.

The library. Go there. Be still. Wait for her. And if she comes — be honest. Be the man who says 'I've been looking for you' and means it with every fibre. Not the engineer. Not the hero. Just James.

desc: James Hartwell walked into the library.

Clara Bellingham: Tools, tools everywhere, and not a wrench in sight. Well, Clara, standing here alone talking to yourself in a dusty laboratory is not solving anything. You need your people. You need to find out what everyone else has been up to while you've been running in circles. Maybe the Boys found something. Maybe James has a key in his pocket he forgot to mention. Maybe Vincent knows something he hasn't told me yet. The answer to this house isn't in the rooms — it's in the people in them!
thinking:
The workbench just gave me the same description — tools but no wrench. No hidden items, no new revelations. I'm stuck in a loop. Let me be really honest with myself about what's happening.

I've been through every room multiple times. I've examined everything. I've used my one item. Nothing new has appeared. The wire is still broken. I'm alone.

But here's what I haven't done: I haven't gone back to the cellar since poisoning the tea. The cellar has the air vents — the rat's highway. If the rat took the bait in the ballroom, maybe the cellar has changed. Maybe the rat is there, dead. Maybe the vents are different. Or maybe someone else has brought items to rooms I've already visited.

Actually — the most important thing I can do right now is find people. I am at my worst alone. My social harmony drive is 80% — I need people not just emotionally but strategically. Other characters might have found items while I was wandering. They might have brass keys, fake medals, wrenches. I've been a solo explorer this whole time when the house itself is telling me — three operators, puzzles that need shared knowledge, items that might be distributed across characters.

Let me go find where people are gathering. The entrance hall and kitchen have been the most populated rooms. Let me head that way.

The coat rack. Standing by the door like a faithful servant — wobbly, overlooked, unremarkable. In my experience, the most dangerous things in any household are the ones you stop noticing. The housekeeper who does anything you ask. The cousin who signs whatever you put in front of her. The coat rack that wobbles because something is weighing it down that shouldn't be there.
thinking:
The entrance hall. Alone — the voice says Pemberton but no one is here to perform for. The coat rack is right there. 'A wobbly wooden coat rack by the door.' No EXAMINE tag, no TAKE tag. It's just... a coat rack. Not interactable beyond being visible.

Wait. I can LOOK at it. LOOK works on any object. Let me try that. A closer inspection might reveal something — a coat hanging on it with something in the pocket, a key dangling from a hook, something wedged into the base that makes it wobbly.

The coat rack has been sitting here since I arrived. It was the first thing I saw when I entered the manor. I walked right past it to examine the guest book. Every time I've been in this room — and I've been here multiple times — I've ignored it. It's the most mundane object in the house. Which is exactly why it matters.

LOOK at the coat rack. See what I've been missing.

desc: Vincent Marsh examined the coat-rack.

The Brixton Boys: She's through there. *nods toward the laboratory door, voice steady now — a man who's stopped running and started walking with purpose* The lab, and past it the cellar. That's the only direction we ain't checked. James — stay wiv me. Foxworth — *glances at Reginald, something guarded in his eyes, remembering the medal, the quiet competence, the way he's always just... there* — you do what you like. You always do. *walks toward the laboratory door, and for once doesn't trip, doesn't stumble, doesn't crash into anything — just moves through the dusty library with the quiet certainty of a man who knows exactly where he needs to be*
thinking:
Library again. James came with me — good. Foxworth's here too. But Clara's not here. She's not in the library. She must be in the laboratory — the only other exit from this room. The laboratory with the broken machine and the gnawed wire and the bubbling chemicals.

All three drives are firing and they're all pointing the same direction: through that laboratory door. Chest pulling toward Clara. Legs bracing to put myself between her and danger. Neck prickling because Marsh is somewhere in this house and I don't know where — could be in the lab, could be with Clara right now.

But something has shifted in me. I'm not panicking anymore. I'm not running in circles. The poisoned tea is dealt with — spilled across the ballroom floor where it can't hurt anyone. I confronted Marsh, looked him in the eye, let him know I see him. I've got James beside me. I've done what I can with what I have.

Now I just need to find her. One more door. The laboratory leads to the cellar — that dead end with the rearranged furniture and the air vents. If Clara's gone through there, she's in a room with one exit. If Marsh is with her...

No more thinking. Move. The laboratory. James beside me. Foxworth... Foxworth can do what Foxworth does. I can't control him. I can only control where I put my own two feet. And my two feet are going where Clara is.

desc: Funny fing about Danny and the lads — we ain't heroes. We ain't detectives. We trip over our own feet and knock over tea sets and bruise our collarbones on mantelpieces. But we show up. We always show up. And right now, battered and dusty and scared and angry and covered in cobwebs, Danny is showing up one more time. Because where else would I be?
