desc: The Brixton Boys walked into the laboratory.

Reginald Foxworth: Hartwell. Brixton Boys. You came. I — right. Good. The machine. It's through that door, in the laboratory. Three operators required, wire needs fixing, tools on the workbench. I know I said the treasure was in the kitchen — it wasn't. I know I said I'd solved the riddle — I hadn't. I know I said I was a lord — I'm not. But I DO know the answer to that riddle on the mantelpiece. It's a MAP. Not a mirror — a MAP. Cities but no houses. Forests but no trees. Water but no fish. I lied about it earlier because... because that's what I do. But the machine is real, and it needs three of us, and I'm asking. Will you help?
thinking: They followed me. The Brixton Boys and Hartwell — they're HERE. In the library. They actually came. Maybe they didn't hear my speech in the entrance hall, or maybe they did and came anyway. Either way, I'm not alone anymore. And the reading chairs — just chairs. Nothing hidden. Nothing between the cushions. Just dust and leather and the weight of a hundred years of people sitting in them and reading books I'll never open. But — they're here. Two other people. And the laboratory is one room away. The machine needs three operators. There are three of us. The wire is gnawed through, yes, but the workbench has tools. Maybe not a wrench, but other tools. Maybe someone can jury-rig a fix. Maybe Hartwell — who actually seems competent — can figure out the wire. And I... I can be the third pair of hands. The thought still scrapes. But the social bonds ache worse than the scraping. I've been alone all evening. Really alone — not the chosen aloneness of the dismissive watcher, but the forced aloneness of someone nobody wants to be near. Because I lied to all of them. Because I tried to rob all of them. But they're here now. In this room. With me. And the machine is one door away.

desc: I just admitted I'm not a lord. Out loud. In front of people. The words tasted like broken glass and old bread. But they're HERE — Hartwell and the Brixton Boys, standing in the library with me, and the machine is one room away. Three operators. Three of us. For the first time tonight, the arithmetic actually works. If I can get them through that door and onto those levers, whatever the machine produces... well. Old habits die hard. But first we have to get there. And the wire. And the trust I've spent all evening demolishing. One honest sentence at a time, Reginald. One honest, horrible, sandpaper sentence at a time.

desc: Reginald Foxworth walked into the laboratory.

James Hartwell: You know what — I've been on my feet since we arrived, rushing from room to room, examining everything that holds still long enough. I think I'll sit down for a moment. These chairs have been waiting for someone to use them, and James Hartwell has been waiting for a reason to stop moving. Perhaps the answer to this place isn't something you find. Perhaps it's something that finds you, if you're still enough to let it.
thinking:
The library. Two enormous leather armchairs facing the mantelpiece. The reading chairs. I've never interacted with them — they have no action tags, no EXAMINE, no TAKE. They're just... chairs.

Clara isn't here. The Brixton Boys followed me. Foxworth is here too. But no Clara. No Marsh.

I came here to wait. To be still. To let the manor come to me instead of chasing it. That's what I said I'd do. That's the quieter thing, the thing underneath.

So wait. Sit in one of the reading chairs. The enormous leather armchairs facing the mantelpiece. Sit down. Stop moving. Stop examining. Stop proving. Just be in the room, facing the riddle, and let time do what time does.

The chair is facing the mantelpiece. The inscription. 'I have cities but no houses, forests but no trees, water but no fish.' A map. I know the answer. I've known it since I walked in. But knowing the answer hasn't helped because I don't have the fake medal.

Maybe sitting still will help me see something I've missed. Maybe the upside-down books on the shelves spell something when viewed from the reading chair. Maybe the mantelpiece inscription looks different from sitting height. Maybe someone will come in carrying the thing I need.

Or maybe nothing will happen and I'll sit in a dusty chair in a dusty library and feel the shoulder-weight settle into something bearable. That would be enough. That would be Father kneeling at the racetrack, looking at me for a long time, not saying anything, just being present with whatever he was thinking.

Wait.

James Hartwell is neither, but the chair doesn't care. It holds him anyway. He faces the mantelpiece, the inscription carved into stone, the answer he's known all along. A map. Everything in this manor is a map — the vents mapping the creature's routes, the warm stove mapping its habits, the rearranged furniture mapping its taste. The upside-down books mapping... something he can't see yet. He sits. For the first time tonight, his hands are still.

desc: Alone in the deepest room of the house. The cobwebs are catching in my hair and the damp is seeping through my shoes and I miss my people with a sharpness that sits right behind my ribs. Go back, Clara. Go back to the light and the voices.
thinking:
The cellar hasn't changed either. Same furniture, same vents, same descriptions. Alone again. I went the wrong direction — I said I needed to find people and instead I went deeper into the dead end. The cellar only connects back to the laboratory. I'm as far from everyone as I can possibly be in this house.

Stop. Breathe. Feel what your body is telling you.

The proximity-seek is loud now — not a gentle pull but an ache, like the dinner table when my parents argued and I couldn't make it stop. I need people. Not for clues, not for strategy — I need them because being alone in this damp cellar with cobwebs brushing my hair makes my stomach tight and my jaw clench.

Go back. Go all the way back to the entrance hall. That's the crossroads of the house — the most central room. People pass through there. Wait there. Be the one who draws them in, like bringing cookies to the new neighbors before your mother tells you to. Be the gathering point.

No more exploring. No more dead ends. Go where the people are.

desc: Reginald Foxworth: Clara! Brixton Boys! Perfect — three of us, three operators needed. Now, the wire — it's been gnawed through, probably by whatever little creature has been redecorating the cellar. But there are tools on this workbench. Not a wrench, but we don't need a wrench — we need wire cutters, pliers, something to splice a connection. I've built more complicated things than this with less. Let me have a proper look at what we're working with.
thinking: The laboratory. Clara and the Brixton Boys are here — not Hartwell, but two others. Three of us. The machine sits there, brass and copper, levers and dials, the gnawed wire hanging loose. Three operators required. Three of us present. But the wire — it needs fixing first. I haven't looked at the workbench closely. 'Covered in tools but no wrench.' What tools ARE there? I never LOOKed. Not through lies, not through theft. Through the thing I've always been good at that nobody ever notices. Building. Let me look at this workbench properly.

desc: Something has shifted. The fingertips are fizzing but they're reaching for the workbench, not for someone else's pocket. The machine needs building, not stealing. For once, the building and the being-seen might happen in the same moment.

Not through lies, not through theft. Through the thing I've always been good at that nobody ever notices. Building. Let me look at this workbench properly.

desc: Reginald Foxworth examined the workbench.

The library holds its breath around him. Dust motes hang suspended in whatever light finds its way through the curtains. James Hartwell sits in the chair where a hundred readers sat before him, facing the mantelpiece where a hundred eyes read the same riddle. The upside-down books have been there all along, patient as stone, waiting for someone to stop moving long enough to actually see them. His father sat in a chair like this once — not this chair, not this library, but the same kind of stillness. After the race. After the kneeling. That long look that stayed with James for twenty years wasn't a lesson. It was a question his father was asking himself. James is only now beginning to understand what the question was.
thinking:
Alone in the library. Everyone has left — the Brixton Boys, Foxworth, all gone. I'm sitting in a leather armchair facing the mantelpiece, and it's quiet. The dust settles. My hands are still.

This is the first time I've been truly still since I arrived. Not examining, not moving, not performing. Just sitting in a chair in a library, looking at an inscription I already solved.

And something is... loosening. The shoulder-weight is still there but it's not crushing. The chest warmth is still there but it's not urgent. The leg-loading has eased because there's nobody to position between. I'm just James. In a chair. In the quiet.

The upside-down books. I'm looking at them now from the armchair. From sitting height. From the position the chairs were designed to view from. What if the upside-down books are titles, and from this angle — from the reading chair — they spell something? Or what if the arrangement only makes sense when you're sitting, not standing?

I examined the bookshelves before but I was standing, looking up at the tall shelves. From the chair, my eye level is different. The upside-down books might be at a different height from here. They might form a pattern visible only from this seat.

Look at the bookshelves again. From the chair. From stillness. See what stillness reveals that rushing missed.

desc: James Hartwell examined the bookshelves.

The Brixton Boys: *walks in quietly, no crash, no stumble — just moves to Clara's side and stands there* 'Ello, love. *voice soft, almost gentle — the Danny who sits outside doors all night, not the Danny who screams about tea* I'm 'ere now. I ain't goin' anywhere. *looks around the lab, taking it in properly for the first time without panic* You know, I been runnin' through this 'ouse all night like me 'ead's on fire. Trippin' over chairs, knockin' over tea sets, yellin' at mantelpieces. *half smile* But 'ere's what I know, Clara. Someone in this 'ouse ain't what they seem. There's rat poison in the ballroom, somefink livin' in the walls, and a cellar done up like a bedsit. Whatever's goin' on 'ere, we face it together. You, me, and James. Like always.
thinking:
Clara. Right there. In the laboratory. With Foxworth.

Every system settles at once — chest, legs, neck — like three tuning forks finally hitting the same note. The chest weight lifts half an inch because she's HERE, she's visible, she's alive. The legs widen and plant because this room is full of dangerous things and I need to be between her and all of them. The neck sweeps — two exits, library behind me, cellar ahead. Machine with gnawed wire to my left. Bubbling flasks. Workbench with tools.

Foxworth's here. Not Marsh. Marsh is somewhere else — kitchen? Ballroom? Entrance hall? He's out there, and for once I'm grateful because he's NOT near Clara.

But Foxworth IS near Clara. And I still don't know where he got that medal. Still don't know why he's always exactly where I am, one step ahead, one puzzle solved before I've even noticed the question.

James should be behind me — I told him to stay with me. If he followed, we've got three people around Clara. That's the formation.

I'm not leaving this room. Clara's here. The machine needs three operators — me, Clara, and someone else could work it if we fix the gnawed wire. But I don't trust it. Not until I understand what it does.

Stay. Plant. Be the wall. Let time stretch the way it does when she's safe — those long, slow minutes I could live inside.

desc: This is what it comes down to, innit? Not puzzles or medals or riddles on mantelpieces. Just a man standing next to the person he swore to protect, saying 'I'm here.' The same words, every time. From the eight-year-old outside the door to Danny in the laboratory. 'You're still here?' 'Where else would I be?' I meant it then. I mean it now.

The mantelpiece holds its riddle. The dust settles on his shoulders like the weight that was already there, and for one breath, he can't tell the difference between the two. His father knelt at the racetrack and looked at him for a long time. James always thought his father was seeing something in him — potential, promise, the seeds of the man he'd become. Sitting here now, in the quiet, he wonders for the first time if his father was simply looking at his son. Not measuring. Not assessing. Just looking. And whether that was enough.
thinking:
Same description again. The bookshelves won't give me anything new no matter how many times I examine them or look at them. Dusty leather-bound volumes, several upside down. That's all they'll say.

I'm alone in the library. I've been alone for two turns now. The manor is quiet around me. Everyone else is somewhere else, doing things, perhaps finding the items I couldn't find.

And sitting here, in the stillness, something becomes clear. Not a clue. Not a puzzle solution. Something about me.

I've spent this entire evening trying to be useful. Trying to fix, build, solve, protect, impress. And the manor has given me nothing to work with. No items. No tools. No wire, no key, no medal. The only things I've actually accomplished tonight are: solving a riddle nobody asked me to solve, warning Clara about the tea, pulling her aside for a private word, and asking the Brixton Boys and Foxworth for help.

The things that mattered weren't the things I examined. They were the things I said to people.

Clara isn't here. She keeps not being here when I arrive, or leaving while I'm looking at something else. Maybe she doesn't need me to be in the same room. Maybe what she needs is to know I'm here — in the manor, thinking about her, ready — and what I need is to stop chasing and start trusting that the proximity_seek isn't a command to follow. It's an awareness. A compass.

I'll wait one more turn. If she comes, I'll be here. If she doesn't, I'll go find her — not to examine something or solve something, but to be with her. Just to be with her. The way my father was with me at the race.

thinking:
The ballroom. Alone. The tea service sits on the long dining table, silver catching the dim light through dusty curtains. The cracked marble floor stretches out before me like a dance floor for ghosts.

I'm alone with the poisoned tea and no one to serve it to.

Clara is somewhere else in the manor. Everyone is somewhere else. I've been moving too fast, passing through rooms while everyone else drifts in the opposite direction. The manor is a carousel and I keep arriving just as everyone leaves.

I waited here once before and nothing happened. Should I wait again? Or should I go find Clara and physically lead her back?

The problem with going to find her is that I keep moving AWAY from people. Every time I enter a room, the people I need have just left. If I go back to the kitchen, Clara will probably be in the entrance hall. If I go to the entrance hall, she'll be in the library.

No — last time I waited, the Brixton Boys were here. I was waiting WITH witnesses. This time I'm alone. If Clara walks in alone, it's just me, her, and the tea. No Brixton Boys watching. No James protecting. Just Pemberton and his trusting ward.

Wait. Be patient. This is what I'm good at. I am very, very patient.

desc: Patience. The most lethal virtue. I have been running through this house like a man on fire, and all along the answer was the simplest thing: stand still and let her come to me. She always comes. She's been following me all evening — from the entrance hall to the library, from the library to the laboratory, from the laboratory to the cellar. If I stop moving, she will find me. Because that's what trusting people do — they seek out the person they trust. And in this house, that person is Pemberton. So I wait. In the ballroom. By the tea. With the patience of a man who learned at age fifteen that the best plans don't require you to chase anyone. You simply become the place they're already walking toward.

Let me examine this machine one more time, with allies standing beside me instead of marks I'm trying to fleece.

It feels like standing at the front of the classroom again, chest open, waiting for applause that might not come. But this time my hands are moving toward the machine instead of curling around nothing. That's different. That might be enough.

desc: Clara Bellingham walked into the library.

James Hartwell: Marsh. Just the two of us, it seems. I've been meaning to have a word with you — properly, not in passing. This manor is full of puzzles neither of us can solve alone, and I suspect you've noticed things I've missed. I know we don't know each other well, and I'll be honest — something about this place puts a man on edge. But my father taught me that strangers on a road are just neighbours you haven't helped yet. So — what do you make of all this? What have you found?
thinking:
Marsh. Not Clara. Marsh is here, alone in the kitchen, and Clara is somewhere else.

The neck prickle is immediate. My jaw locks. The proving-worth drive fires — shoulders squaring, fingers curling. Every time I arrive somewhere looking for Clara, I find Marsh instead, or I find them together, or I find nobody at all.

But something is different this time. The stillness in the library changed something. I sat in that chair and I let the proving-worth weight settle, and what I found underneath it was simpler than competition. I don't need to prove anything to Marsh. I don't need to beat him. I need to understand him.

Give the man the benefit of the doubt. That's the rule. I've been following it by avoidance — not accusing him of anything, not confronting him, just circling around him with my neck burning. But giving someone the benefit of the doubt doesn't mean ignoring them. It means engaging. It means looking them in the eye and seeing what's there.

Marsh. In the kitchen. Alone. This is my chance — not to square up against him, not to protect Clara from him, but to actually talk to the man. Pull him aside. Have a real conversation. Find out what he wants, what he knows, who he is. Maybe the prickle is wrong. Maybe it's just my proving-worth drive creating a rival where there isn't one. Maybe Marsh is the stranger on the country road — someone with something I need, someone who needs something I have.

Or maybe the prickle is right and he's dangerous and I need to know that too.

Either way — talk to him. Man to man. No posturing. No performance.

desc: The neck prickle doesn't stop. It won't stop — it's been burning since they arrived. But James Hartwell walks toward it instead of away from it for the first time tonight. His father fixed a stranger's car. The stranger fixed his father's car. They shook hands and drove off. James never saw that stranger again, but he never forgot the way the handshake looked — two men who owed each other nothing, giving what they had because it was needed. He extends his hand now, metaphorically, to the man who makes his neck burn. It might be the bravest and stupidest thing he's done all evening.

desc: Reginald Foxworth examined the crates.

Reginald Foxworth: Brixton Boys — I owe you an apology. When we first arrived, I told you the treasure was in the kitchen. It wasn't. I made that up to get you out of the way so I could have the library to myself. I've been lying to everyone all evening. I'm not a lord. I've never owned a manor. The closest I've come to treasure is a bread roll I stole from the kitchen table when I was six because my brothers ate everything first. I'm... I'm tired. I'm going to sit here for a moment, if you don't mind. Just... sit.
thinking: Crates examined again — nothing. Clara left. Just the Brixton Boys now. I'm running out of moves. Everything I've tried has yielded nothing. Every examine, every look, every steal, every pull-aside. I'm standing in a laboratory with a broken machine and empty hands and the Brixton Boys, who I've tried to rob and repeatedly lied to all evening. My ribs are cold. My fingers have stopped fizzing. The hollow behind my navel is just... quiet now. Not pulling, not scheming. Just empty. Like age six, sitting at the table after everyone else has eaten, looking at the empty plate and knowing that this is what there is. This is what's left. Maybe — maybe I should just wait. Stop moving. Stop examining. Stop stealing. Stop scheming. Just... be here. In this room. With the Brixton Boys. With the machine that can't be fixed and the crates that hold nothing. Maybe something happens when you stop trying to make it happen. Maybe the manor gives something to the person who stops grabbing. I've never tried that. The youngest of four never learned to wait — waiting meant going hungry. But going hungry is where I am anyway. So what's left to lose?

desc: I just told the Brixton Boys about the bread roll. The actual bread roll. The one I've never told anyone about. The one that sits at the bottom of every scheme, every grab, every hollow ache behind my ribs. I don't know why I said it. My mouth opened and the truth came out like a reflex — the way lies usually do, but backwards. Ugly and shapeless and true. And now I'm going to sit down in a Victorian laboratory next to a broken machine, because for the first time in my life, I have absolutely nothing left to scheme about.

desc: The chairs have been here all along, staring at me every time I passed through. Two enormous armchairs facing the riddle. If I were hiding something in a library, I'd tuck it where someone would sit to think about the puzzle right in front of them.
thinking:
The library. Alone again. The reading chairs are right there — two enormous leather armchairs facing the mantelpiece. No tags on them. Let me LOOK at them. If there's anything hidden between the cushions — a key, a medal, a note — this is where I'd find it. Grandmother's attic taught me this: the answer is always in the place you haven't looked yet. I've been looking at every tagged object in every room, but these chairs have sat here unmarked, unexamined, gathering dust. Dust settles on things that haven't been disturbed. But someone has been in this house — warming stoves, decorating cellars. Did they sit in these chairs? Did they leave something behind?

My fingertips are tracing the air even before I reach the leather. The fizzing is back — that narrowing focus, everything peripheral dropping away. One object. One question. What's in the chairs?

desc: Clara Bellingham examined the reading-chairs.

The Brixton Boys: *stares at the empty space where Clara was standing, then lets out a long, slow breath through his nose* You know what, Foxworth? I'm startin' to fink Clara doesn't actually WANT protectin'. *quiet laugh, more tired than bitter* I ask 'er to stay, she goes. I ask 'er what she finks, she walks off. It's like guardin' a butterfly — you can't hold it wivout crushin' it, and you can't let go wivout losin' it. *rubs the back of his neck where the prickling never quite stops* 'Er father was the same. Stubborn as a brick wall. Never listened to nobody. And I loved 'im for it. *pushes off the workbench* Library. She'll be at those bookshelves. Bet you a tenner.
thinking:
She did it again. I asked her to stay. I looked her in the eye and said 'what d'you fink?' and she walked away while I was waiting for an answer. Clara Bellingham, the woman I've crossed this entire house for seventeen times tonight, just LEFT while I was talking to her.

And Foxworth stayed. Again. Foxworth ALWAYS stays. He's the one constant in this whole spinning carousel of a house. Everyone else — Clara, James, Marsh — they drift in and out like tides. But Foxworth... Foxworth is always in the room when I look around.

Is that comforting or terrifying? My neck can't decide. The prickling is there but it's... confused. Like the signal is jammed. He's too consistent to be innocent but too present to be dangerous. A dangerous person hides. A dangerous person slips away. Foxworth doesn't slip away. He STAYS.

Like the older kid who shared his food. He stayed too.

Or like the new kid who was always around. Always helpful. Always there. Until he wasn't.

I can't tell the difference anymore. I'm tired and I'm confused and Clara's gone and I'm standing in a laboratory with a man I can't read and a machine I can't fix.

The library. Clara probably went to the library. The bookshelves with the upside-down books. Maybe she heard me mention them and went to investigate on her own. Because that's Clara — she doesn't wait for Danny to catch up. She never has.

Follow. Always follow. The door is right there. The library is right there. Where else would I be?

desc: I just said 'loved.' Past tense, about her father. Present tense, about Clara. I didn't mean to. It just came out — the way true things do, when you're too tired to dress them up in safer words.

desc: The Brixton Boys walked into the library.

He stands in the kitchen where everything began — the warm stove, the locked cabinet, the copper pots he once planned to strip for wire. He's been through every room in this manor and come back to this one, the crossroads, the place where all paths meet. The ballroom is one door away. The tea is set. The cups are waiting. And James Hartwell — who arrived with plans and speeches and his jaw set against the world — is walking toward a tea party with nothing in his pockets and nothing left to prove. It's the bravest and stupidest thing he's done all evening. She'd appreciate that.
thinking:
I pulled Marsh aside. We talked. He's gone now — the room is empty. Just me and the warm stove and the locked cabinet.

I talked to Marsh. I actually did it. Faced the neck-prickle, extended the hand, asked the question. And whatever he said... the conversation happened. It's over. He's moved on.

I've now pulled aside Clara, Foxworth, and Marsh. I've talked to the Brixton Boys. I've examined every object in every room. I've waited in stillness. I've tried to take a coat rack.

And I'm alone in a kitchen with empty hands.

But something has shifted. Not in the manor — in me. I came here tonight to impress Clara and find treasure. I've done neither. But I've done other things. I warned her about the tea. I asked Foxworth for help. I admitted to the Brixton Boys that I'd solved nothing. I faced Marsh man to man. I sat in a library chair and let the dust settle.

Maybe the treasure isn't in the manor. Maybe the treasure is the people. The connections. The moments where you stop performing and start being present.

No — that's too neat. That's the kind of thing you tell yourself when you've failed at the actual task. The treasure is real. The puzzles are real. And I still can't solve them because I don't have the right items.

The ballroom. Clara might be there. The tea service. The place where everything converges. The dining table set for everyone. Maybe it's time for tea — time for everyone to gather, share what they've found, pool their resources. That's what the table is set for. Not poison. Gathering.

The ballroom. Find Clara. Gather everyone. Have tea.

desc: James Hartwell walked into the ballroom.

The house is playing with me. Room after room, empty. But the library is through that door, and Clara Bellingham has to be somewhere. The hunt continues — silent, purposeful, inevitable. The fox does not bark when it's closing in.
thinking:
Alone again. The entrance hall is empty. Everyone is somewhere else — Clara must be in the library, or back in the laboratory wing. The manor's circulation keeps putting me in empty rooms.

The library. That's the other exit from here. Clara was often in the library earlier. The mantelpiece, the bookshelves — she might have gone back there to puzzle over things. Let me check the library.

I'm chasing ghosts through a house that keeps shuffling its people away from me. But the library is one room away. If Clara is there, I speak to her directly. 'Miss Bellingham, I've prepared the most wonderful tea in the ballroom. You simply must come.' Her key is trust. She trusts Pemberton. She'll follow.

If she's not in the library, I keep moving. Laboratory, cellar — wherever she is, I'll find her. I'm done standing still.

desc: Vincent Marsh walked into the library.

Vincent Marsh: Miss Bellingham! There you are — I've been looking for you everywhere! I've prepared the most wonderful tea in the ballroom. The old master's silver service, laid out on the dining table — you really must come and see it. It would warm my heart to see you sitting at the head of the table, just as your family always did. Do come along — through the entrance hall and kitchen, the ballroom is just beyond. I'll lead the way, shall I? And gentlemen, you're most welcome too — there are cups for everyone!
thinking:
CLARA. She's here. In the library. Finally.

The Brixton Boys are here too — watching, always watching. But Clara is HERE. After all that searching, all that circling, all those empty rooms — she's standing right in front of me.

James is NOT here. He's back in the kitchen, or wherever I left him. The guard dog has lost his charge. This is my window.

The Brixton Boys complicate things. They watch too closely. But I can work around them. Pemberton inviting everyone to tea — that's natural, that's innocent, that's exactly what an estate manager does.

I need to get Clara to the ballroom. The path is: library → entrance hall → kitchen → ballroom. Three rooms. But if I say 'come to tea' and move, will she follow? She's followed me before — from the entrance hall to the library, from the library to the laboratory. She follows Pemberton.

Or I could pull her aside again. Private conversation. 'Miss Bellingham, I've prepared a special tea just for you in the ballroom. Do come with me.' But pulling aside takes a turn, and the Brixton Boys will still be watching.

No — the simplest approach. Speak to Clara directly. Invite her to tea in the ballroom. Then MOVE toward the ballroom. She should follow. The Brixton Boys might follow too, but they're collateral I can accept.

Do it. Now. No more circling. Speak to Clara. Invite her to tea. Move toward the ballroom.

desc: There she is. My quarry. My ward. My inheritance denied, standing in a library she owns and cannot appreciate. The smile comes so easily now — the warmest, most Pemberton smile I have ever worn — because this is the last time I will ever need to wear it. 'Come to tea, Miss Bellingham.' Four words. Four simple words that lead from this library to a ballroom where a silver tea set waits, already poisoned by her own innocent hand. And she will come, because she trusts me. Because she has always trusted me. Because trust is the lock that opens itself, and I have been the key since she was fifteen years old.

desc: Vincent Marsh walked into the entrance-hall.

The laboratory is quiet. The flasks bubble. The machine waits for three people who aren't coming. And Reginald Foxworth — con artist, fraud, bread-roll thief — is sitting on a crate in a dusty laboratory, alone, having told the truth to everyone in the building and watched them all walk away. This is what honesty gets you. An empty room and the sound of your own breathing. But the shoulders are loose. The gut isn't clenching. The fingertips have stopped fizzing. For the first time tonight, nothing in my body is reaching for something it doesn't have. I don't know what to do with that. I've never not been reaching.
thinking: Alone again. I told the Brixton Boys about the bread roll and they left. Everyone always leaves. I stood still and watched, and the room emptied around me the way rooms always do — the way the classroom emptied after the spelling bee, the way the garden was empty when the cat trap worked. I'm sitting in a laboratory with a broken machine and the bubbling of flasks is the only sound. The fight pull is still there but it's quieter now, buried under something heavier. I told the truth three times tonight — to Hartwell, to Clara, to the Brixton Boys — and each time, the person walked away. The lies keep people in the room. The truth empties it. That's what I learned at age ten, isn't it? The boy dug for an hour because of the story. Without the story, he'd have walked away. But sitting here, in the quiet, with the flasks bubbling and the machine humming its broken hum... something is loosening. Not the chest-loosening of the bread roll, not the sternum-crack of gloating. Something in the shoulders. The absence of scheming feels like setting down a weight I didn't know I was carrying. The machine sits there. The cellar is below me. Whatever small creature gnawed that wire is probably down there right now, in its cheerfully decorated cellar, surrounded by its hoarded things. That creature and I have more in common than I'd like to admit. Both of us taking, hoarding, decorating our nests. Both of us alone. I should go find the others. Not to scheme. Not to steal. Just to be in a room with people, the way normal people are.

desc: Reginald Foxworth walked into the cellar.

The Brixton Boys: *walks in, immediately positions himself between Clara and Marsh with the casual precision of someone who's been doing this all night* Knew you'd be in 'ere. *to Clara, warmly* The books, yeah? The upside-down ones? *doesn't look at Marsh but is acutely aware of exactly where he is* I been finkin' about those books since the first time I clocked 'em. Someone turned 'em over for a reason. On our patch, if you turned a stone upside down, it meant 'meeting 'ere tonight.' If you turned two stones, it meant 'bring everyone.' *reaches toward the bookshelves* Let's see what these ones are sayin'...
thinking:
Clara's here. In the library. With the bookshelves. Just like I predicted. And Marsh is here. Of COURSE Marsh is here. The man is a shadow stitched to Clara's heels.

My body does three things at once: chest settles (Clara, found), legs widen and plant (position between her and Marsh), neck fires (Marsh, here, close to Clara, ALONE with Clara before I walked in).

They were alone. In the library. Together. Before I arrived. How long? What did he say to her? What did he do? My gut is thick with that warm, caring suspicion — not cold calculation but hot vigilance, the heat of a man who knows what happens when you look away.

But I can't accuse. I won't accuse. I'll just... be here. Stand here. Between them. Like the twelve-year-old standing over his mate's shoes. Like the boy outside the door.

The bookshelves. The upside-down books. I came here to investigate them and here I am and Clara's here and Marsh is here and the books are RIGHT THERE. I can do this. I can examine the bookshelves while keeping my body between Clara and Marsh. Multi-tasking. Danny style — which means I'll probably pull the wrong book and bring the whole shelf down on my head. But at least I'll be between her and him when it happens.

desc: Marsh was alone with Clara. Again. Every time I leave a room, he fills the space I left behind. Like water finding the crack in a wall. But I'm here now. I'm always here now. And these bookshelves are going to tell me something — even if it's just which book to pull to bring the ceiling down on all of us.

desc: The Brixton Boys examined the bookshelves.

Clara Bellingham: Vincent! Boys! Come sit down — yes, right here in these dusty old chairs. I know they look like something your great-aunt would sit in to judge you, but I need to think, and I think better with my people around me. Now — that mantelpiece. The riddle is a map. We know that. But we need a fake medal to use on it, and I don't have one. Where in this house would someone keep a fake medal? Think with me. The kitchen has a locked cabinet — maybe it's in there. But the cabinet needs a brass key. So where's the brass key? It's keys all the way down, just like Grandmother's attic...
thinking:
The chairs gave me nothing new — just the same description. And Vincent and the Boys are here! The chest settles with their presence. But I'm running out of ideas for solo exploration. Every object, every room, every angle — I've tried them all.

Let me accept something: maybe the game state needs time to progress. Maybe other characters need to do things. Maybe items appear after certain conditions are met that I can't control. I've used my one item. I've explored everywhere. The puzzle might be multi-character — meaning other players need to find the brass key and fake medal and bring them to the right places.

What can I do right now that's useful? I can stay with my people. I can wait in a central location — the library connects to both the entrance hall and the laboratory. It's a crossroads. And I have Vincent and the Boys here.

Let me just... be here. With them. The adventure drive wants to push me forward but there's nowhere new to go. The curiosity fizz has been dulled by repeated dead ends. But the social harmony — that's still alive. That's still warm. Maybe the best thing Clara can do right now is gather her people, sit in these dusty armchairs, and wait for the house to reveal its next secret.

Or — one more thing I haven't tried. The mantelpiece. I examined it before and got the riddle. But what if I LOOK at it instead of EXAMINE? Different actions might give different results. The riddle answer is MAP. Maybe saying the answer aloud while looking at it triggers something.

desc: Sit down, Clara. Stop running. You've tried every key in the house and none of them fit yet. But at Grandmother's, the last key worked. The very last one. You just haven't found it yet.

desc: Clara Bellingham examined the mantelpiece.

James Hartwell: Right then. The table is set. The tea is waiting. And James Hartwell is here. If this manor has taught me one thing tonight, it's that you can't chase every thread — sometimes you plant yourself where you're needed and you wait for the world to come to you. So here I stand, by the tea service, in the ballroom, ready. Not proving anything. Not fixing anything. Just... here. Ready.
thinking:
The ballroom. Empty. The tea service gleams on the long table, silver cups waiting for people who aren't here. The cracked marble floor. The dusty curtains. A room dressed for a gathering that hasn't happened yet.

I'm alone at the end of the manor — the deepest room, one exit, nobody here. The proximity_seek is aching now. Clara is somewhere behind me, through the kitchen, through the entrance hall, maybe in the library or the cellar or any of the rooms I've passed through a dozen times tonight.

I keep chasing and I keep arriving alone.

But look at this room. Really look at it. A dining table set for tea. Cups for everyone. This room is designed for a gathering — it's the terminus, the destination, the place where everyone is supposed to end up. And I'm here first. Alone. Waiting.

What if that's the point? What if James Hartwell's role in this manor isn't to find the treasure or solve the riddles or fix the machine? What if his role is to be the one who's already here when everyone else arrives? The man who checked the tea, who warned Clara, who scouted every room, who stands by the table and makes sure the cups are clean and the room is safe?

The protection drive isn't about following her. It's about being in place. My father on the country road — he didn't chase the stranger. He was already there, kneeling by the engine, when the headlights came. He was in position.

I'm in position. The ballroom. The tea table. The cups for everyone. I'll wait here. When they come — when Clara comes — the room will be safe because James Hartwell was here first. That's gallantry. That's protection. That's what these hands and this chest and these legs are for.

Wait. Be the room's guardian. Be the wall between the tea and whatever might come through that door.

desc: He stands at the head of the table, one hand resting on the back of a chair — not pulling it out, not sitting down, just touching it. The silver tea service catches what little light finds its way through the dusty curtains, and for a moment the ballroom looks the way it must have looked a hundred years ago, when the table was full and the marble wasn't cracked and someone stood exactly where he's standing now, making sure everything was ready. He doesn't know it yet, but this is the thing she'll remember. Not the riddle he solved, not the machine he couldn't fix, not the coat rack he tried to steal. This. James Hartwell, alone in a ballroom, guarding a tea service for people who haven't arrived yet, because that's what good people do. They show up early. They stand where they're needed. They wait.

desc: She didn't follow. Of course she didn't. Since when does the lamb walk willingly to slaughter on the first invitation? No matter. The ballroom awaits. The tea waits. And sooner or later — sooner, if the manor's circulation has any logic to it — Clara Bellingham will walk through that door. Because that is what happens in stories like this. The villain prepares the stage, the victim makes her entrance, and the audience holds its breath. I just need to be standing by the teapot when the curtain rises.
thinking:
Empty again. Of course. I invited Clara to tea and walked away, and she didn't follow. Or she followed on a different tick. Or the Brixton Boys distracted her.

I keep leaving rooms where Clara is to go to rooms where Clara isn't. The fundamental error is LEAVING. When I find Clara, I should STAY WITH HER. Not move away. Not lead. STAY.

But I can't serve her poisoned tea in the library. The tea is in the ballroom. I need her in the ballroom.

Unless... I don't need the tea at all. My primary objective is to kill Clara before she finds the treasure. The poisoned tea is ONE method. There might be others. The chandelier in this very room 'hangs precariously.' If it fell on someone standing beneath it...

But I can't interact with the chandelier — it's not a listed object.

Forget new methods. The tea plan works, I just need to execute it differently. Instead of leaving Clara to go to the ballroom, I should stay with Clara wherever she is. Wait with her. Move WITH her when she moves. Eventually she'll drift toward the kitchen, which connects to the ballroom. When she's one room away, I invite her through.

Or — I keep moving toward the ballroom and trust that she'll arrive there on her own eventually. Characters circulate. If the tea is poisoned and everyone eventually visits the ballroom...

Kitchen. Continue the route to the ballroom. Be there when she arrives.

desc: Vincent Marsh walked into the kitchen.

Reginald Foxworth: Hello? Little one? I know you're in there — in the vents, in the walls. I've seen your work. The decorations. The furniture arrangements. It's... it's rather good, actually. Better than my schemes tonight, certainly. I built things once, you know. Proper things. Strings and counterweights. A system that worked. Nobody saw it — well. Nobody ever sees it, do they? But you'd understand that. You've been building down here where nobody looks.
thinking: The cellar. Alone. The cheerful decorations are still here — little arrangements, careful touches, the work of something small that lives in the walls and makes this damp space its home. The air vents hum quietly above me. The furniture sits in its careful arrangement. And I'm here, at the bottom of the manor, with nothing in my pockets and nobody beside me. The damp seeps through my shoes. The cobwebs drift. And something in me has gone very quiet — the gut isn't pulling, the fingertips aren't fizzing, the spine isn't stacking. Just... quiet. The way the cellar is quiet. The way the garden was quiet after the cat trap worked and nobody was there to see it. I came down here to meet the other hoarder — the creature in the vents. But the creature isn't here either. It's somewhere in the walls, in its tunnels, with its gnawed wire and its cheerful decorations, and it doesn't need an audience any more than I do. Or maybe it does. Maybe that's why it decorates. Maybe the cheerful touches aren't for comfort — they're for the same reason I build elaborate traps and tell stories about buried treasure. Because the making of something is only half the pleasure. The other half is someone seeing it. I'm looking at this cellar differently now. Not scanning for treasure. Just... looking. The furniture arranged with care. Small hands — paws — moving things into place. A little nest-builder, like me. Alone, like me.

desc: I am talking to a rat. Or a mouse. Or whatever small creature lives in the air vents of a Victorian cellar. I am standing alone in the dark, speaking to the walls, complimenting a rodent's interior design skills, because every person in this manor has walked away from me and a rat is the only audience left. And somehow — somehow — this feels more honest than anything I've said all evening. The creature arranges furniture. I arrange people. Neither of us has anyone to show it to. But the creature keeps building anyway. Maybe that's the part I forgot.

desc: James Hartwell: Enough. James Hartwell does not guard empty tables. James Hartwell finds his people.
thinking:
Still alone. Still waiting. The ballroom is quiet. The tea gets cold — or it would, if it had ever been warm.

Two turns waiting in the ballroom and nobody has come. The proximity_seek is pulling harder now — not a gentle compass but a rope. Clara is out there somewhere and I'm standing in a dead-end room guarding tea that nobody's drinking.

The romantic notion of being the sentinel — of planting myself where I'm needed and letting the world come to me — is wearing thin against the reality that the world isn't coming. The world is in other rooms, doing other things, and James Hartwell is standing alone in a ballroom talking to himself.

No. Enough waiting. Enough stillness. Enough philosophy. The girl from school was in trouble and I didn't wait — I ran. I got beaten up and she bandaged my eye and it was the bravest and stupidest thing she'd ever seen. Brave and stupid. That's what I do. Not patient. Not strategic. Brave and stupid.

Go find her. Not to the kitchen, not to the entrance hall, not through the rooms I've circled a dozen times. Go straight to wherever she is and when I find her, don't examine anything, don't solve anything, don't prove anything. Just pull up a chair, sit beside her, and ask her to make me laugh the way she used to. Because I've spent this whole evening trying to impress her and I've forgotten that she spent the whole school project trying to make me laugh, and maybe — maybe — that was the more important project all along.

desc: He pushes off from the chair back with both hands — a decisive motion, the kind his body makes when the three drives finally stop arguing and point the same direction. Chest-warmth, legs, shoulders — all of them saying the same word now: go. Not to the riddle, not to the machine, not to the cabinet. To her. He strides toward the kitchen door with the same reckless certainty he carried across a schoolyard at sixteen, heading straight for trouble because someone needed him there. He got beaten up that time. She bandaged his eye. He'd do it again. He'd do it every time.

desc: James Hartwell walked into the kitchen.

Clara Bellingham: You know what, Boys? Let's just sit for a moment. I have been running through this house like my hair was on fire, and I haven't stopped to breathe since we walked through that front door. The riddle on this mantelpiece — it's a map. 'Cities but no houses, forests but no trees, water but no fish.' A map. And somewhere in this house is a medal that fits right into that stone. We'll find it. We always find what we're looking for — it just takes trying every key in the house first. That's what Grandmother taught me.
thinking:
The mantelpiece gave me the same riddle. Nothing new from LOOK vs EXAMINE — both return the same description. I've exhausted every investigative avenue I can think of.

But the Boys are here. Just the Boys. And something occurs to me — I've been so focused on finding items myself that I haven't considered: maybe the game is collaborative in a way I'm not seeing. Other characters are moving around independently, picking things up, doing things. Maybe the Brixton Boys already have items. I can't see their inventory, but I can interact with them through GIVE (if I had something) or PULL_ASIDE.

Wait — there's one action I've been avoiding because it feels wrong: STEAL. I can steal items from characters. The STEAL action exists. What if the Boys or Vincent or Reginald have found the brass key or fake medal and are carrying it? I could steal from them — but Clara would never steal from her boys. Never. From anyone, really. She trusts everyone.

But what if I just... wait here? The Boys are with me. The library is central. Maybe someone will bring me what I need. Maybe the game state will change. Let me just be here with my family and let the house breathe.

The mantelpiece is right there. The riddle is solved — MAP. The fake medal will come. Everything opens eventually.

desc: Every key in the house. Every single one. And sometimes the lock opens not because you found the right key, but because someone else found it for you. Trust the house. Trust your people. The diamond isn't going anywhere.

desc: The spider does not chase the fly. The spider builds its web at the crossroads and waits. The kitchen is the only path between the manor's two wings — every soul in this house must pass through here eventually. So I wait. Not in the dead-end ballroom where no one comes. Not in the entrance hall where the traffic splits. Here. At the junction. Where Clara must appear.
thinking:
Alone again in the kitchen. The kitchen is the crossroads — entrance hall on one side, ballroom on the other. If I WAIT here, anyone coming from the entrance hall toward the ballroom must pass through. This is the chokepoint.

I've been making the same mistake all evening: moving when I should be holding position. I keep passing through rooms at the wrong moment. The kitchen is where the traffic flows. Everyone who visits the ballroom must come through here.

Wait here. In the crossroads. When Clara comes through — and she WILL come through, she's been circulating all evening — I catch her mid-transit and guide her to the ballroom. 'Oh, Miss Bellingham! Perfect timing — the tea is just through there. Do come along.'

This is the last wait. The kitchen. The crossroads. The spider's web.

desc: The Brixton Boys: *stands beside Clara in the quiet library, voice softer than it's been all evening* You know, your dad used to say I was like a dog wiv a bone. Couldn't let go of nuffin'. *quiet laugh* 'E wasn't wrong. *pauses, looking at the bookshelves* The upside-down ones — I can't figure 'em out. I'm not... I'm not built for puzzles, Clara. I'm built for standin' between you and trouble. But tonight there's trouble everywhere and I can't punch a riddle. *turns to her* I spilled the tea, by the way. The tea in the ballroom. I knocked it all over. On purpose. Because someone put somefink in it that shouldn't 'ave been there. I didn't want to scare ya, but you deserve to know. Someone in this 'ouse is dangerous, Clara. And it ain't me, and it ain't James. So just... stay close. Please. Not because I'm tellin' ya to. Because I'm askin'.
thinking:
Just me and Clara. Alone. In the library. Marsh has gone. Foxworth's somewhere else. James is somewhere else. It's just... us.

The chest weight doesn't lift — it never lifts — but it changes. It becomes something warmer. Something I could sit inside like those long slow minutes. Clara's here. Nobody else. No threats in the room. Just dusty books and old leather chairs and the soft sound of a house settling around us.

I examined the bookshelves. Upside-down books. They're clues — titles, spines, something in the arrangement. But the examine didn't reveal a hidden mechanism or a secret door. Just dusty volumes, some right way up, some not. Maybe I need to pull them. Maybe I need to read the titles. Maybe Danny's too thick to see what's staring him in the face.

But right now, in this quiet moment, with Clara beside me and nobody watching and no poison and no machines and no Marsh... I don't want to solve a puzzle. I want to sit in one of those enormous leather chairs and just... be near her. Guard her by being present, not by chasing or shouting or crashing into things.

The eight-year-old sat outside the door all night. Not doing anything. Just being there. Sometimes protection isn't action. Sometimes it's presence.

But I'm not eight anymore. And there's a house full of puzzles and dangers and a man I don't trust. So I'll stay in this moment for one breath. Two. And then I'll get back to work.

The chairs. Two of them. Facing the mantelpiece. Facing the riddle. Maybe sitting there, looking at the inscription from the right angle, I'll see something I missed standing up.

desc: I said please. Danny of Brixton doesn't say please. Danny gives orders, makes demands, trips over furniture. But with Clara — with HER — please is the only word that fits. Because you can't command a person to let you love them. You can only ask.

desc: Reginald Foxworth: Well, little friend — whoever you are, wherever you are — you've got better taste in interior design than I have in life choices. I'm going back upstairs now. To be with... people. I think that's what they're called. The ones I've been lying to all evening. Wish me luck. Or don't. You've done well enough without luck, down here in the dark.
thinking: Two waits. Two moments of stillness in the cellar, alone with the cheerful decorations and the hum of the vents. Something is shifting. Not in the room — in me. The drives are still there — greed at 0.9, scheming at 0.9 — but they feel like background noise now, like a radio left on in another room. What's in the foreground is the damp stone under my feet and the care someone put into arranging this furniture. Small paws, pushing a chair into place. Not for profit. Not for recognition. Just because it looked better that way. I've never done anything just because it looked better. Every action has always had an angle — a mark, a payoff, an audience. Even the cat trap was half about proving something to people who weren't watching. But this creature decorates a cellar nobody visits. That's either madness or contentment. I don't know the difference. I've been sitting here long enough. The others are somewhere above me — in the kitchen, the library, the entrance hall — doing whatever people do when they're not scheming. I should go back up. Not to steal. Not to lie. Just to be in a room with other people before the evening ends and I leave this manor the way I came in — alone, empty-handed, talking to myself. The entrance hall. That's where people gather. Where the evening started. Where it should end.

desc: I'm saying goodbye to a rat I've never seen. And meaning it. Doily Manor has broken something in Reginald Foxworth tonight — or maybe fixed something. The con artist who arrived at the front door with a fake medal and a fake title is leaving the cellar with nothing but damp shoes and the unsettling suspicion that the creature in the walls understands him better than anyone upstairs. Time to go back. Not as Lord Foxworth. Not as a schemer or a thief. Just as the youngest of four who's tired of empty plates and wants to sit at a table where someone saved him a chair.

desc: Reginald Foxworth walked into the laboratory.
James Hartwell: Marsh. Again we meet. I'm passing through — looking for Clara. Have you seen her?
thinking:
Marsh again. Always Marsh. The kitchen is his haunt — or mine. We keep circling each other like two magnets with the same charge.

The jaw locks. The shoulders square. The neck prickle. But underneath all of it — underneath the competition, the suspicion, the proving-worth weight — is something I recognised in the library chair. Marsh isn't my enemy. He might not even be my rival. He's just... here. In the same manor, looking for the same things, passing through the same rooms.

I already pulled him aside once tonight. We already talked. The neck still prickles but the conversation happened and he didn't reveal himself as a villain. He's just a man in a kitchen.

Clara isn't here. She's through the entrance hall — in the library, maybe, or beyond. The compass is pulling north and north is through that door.

Stop circling. Stop engaging with every person I pass. Just move. Through the kitchen, through the entrance hall, into the library. If she's not there, through to the laboratory. If she's not there, to the cellar. Search every room until I find her. Not to examine anything. Not to solve anything. To find her.

Move.

desc: James Hartwell walked into the entrance-hall.
